items.evidenceFor: sleeping a little better after 6 to 12 weeks
items.evidenceSummary: Five small trials, all run in India, found sleep improved modestly after 6 to 12 weeks, more so in people with insomnia. Stress scores eased too. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported.
items.humanQuestion: Do you take it more for stress or for sleep?
items.notesInternal: Area kept as sleep for this batch, but stress is at least as common a reason to buy it (also_serves mind). If a reviewer moves it to mind, the stress evidence grades similarly (Akhgarjand 2022: 12 RCTs, 1,002 adults, low certainty). Tier B with caveats: all five pooled sleep trials ran in India; in the two KSM-66 trials I checked (Langade 2019, Salve 2019) the extract was supplied by its maker (Ixoreal) with no funding statement, the other two KSM-66 trials (Kelgane 2020, Langade 2021) were not checked, and the Shoden trial was sponsored by its maker (Arjuna). No trial declared brand funding outright, so it is not N, but independent replication outside India is missing. Cheah 2021 rated the overall sleep evidence moderate certainty. Sensoril has no trial in the sleep meta-analysis. dose_min 250 mg applies to KSM-66 (Salve 2019); Shoden worked at 120 mg, so the floor depends on the extract; plain root powder was not studied. V3's 6 to 8 week framing was roughly right; its liver and thyroid flags are confirmed. Safety sources: LiverTox (captcha) and NIH ODS (HTTP 403) could not be opened, so the liver rows rest on Bjornsson 2020 and Philips 2023, the thyroid row on Sharma 2018, and the pregnancy row on standard label warnings. Regulatory context, not cited as evidence: Denmark banned it in supplements in 2023 and the Dutch RIVM advised against it in 2024 (NutraIngredients timeline, July 2026). Cost is an estimate.

safety.note: Safety while breastfeeding is not established, so a clinician's view comes first.
Rare liver injury has been reported, and it was most serious in people with existing liver disease.
In a small trial it shifted thyroid hormone levels, so thyroid medicine calls for a clinician check first.
Product labels warn against use during pregnancy.

items.name: Mouth tape
items.evidenceFor: better sleep in people without sleep apnea
items.evidenceSummary: A 2025 review found ten small, low-quality studies, mostly in people with sleep apnea or mouth breathing; a few saw less snoring. None tested people who sleep normally, and taping is risky with a blocked nose.
items.humanQuestion: Do you snore, or is it more about dry mouth?
items.originQuestion: Where did you first hear about mouth tape?
items.notesInternal: V3 graded C off one small uncontrolled study in mild apnea (Lee 2022: 20 people, no control group). Rhee 2025 (systematic review) found ten poor-quality studies, none testing normal sleepers, and concluded the data do not support taping. Graded D for better sleep in people without sleep apnea (mechanism and anecdote only); the snoring signal in mild apnea is C at best. The main risks (blocked nose, moderate or severe apnea, regurgitation while taped) have no matching condition in the brief's safety list. Suggest adding a 'sleep-apnea-or-blocked-nose' condition with never-suggest, and a gate that routes loud snoring, gasping or witnessed breathing pauses to a clinician. Cost is an estimate (branded strips cost more, plain surgical tape far less).

safety.note: No studies include children, and taping carries breathing risks.

items.name: Eight Sleep / cooling mattress pad
items.evidenceFor: a little more deep sleep
items.evidenceSummary: The only studies of the product itself come from the company. In one blinded trial, a cooler mattress added about 7 minutes of deep sleep and a slightly slower heart rate. Heat disturbs sleep, so hot sleepers may gain most.
items.humanQuestion: Do you sleep hot, and is the cooling still on?
items.fitsInstead: A fan, lighter bedding and a cooler room, for far less.
items.notesInternal: Product-specific evidence is brand-funded only (Moyen 2024: nine of ten authors are Eight Sleep staff, fixed off-on-off order, no randomization, deep and REM gains only in sex and time-of-night subgroups), which alone would be N. The C rests on Herberger 2024 (randomized, blinded crossover, one night per mattress, +7.5 min deep sleep, about 2 bpm lower heart rate), whose co-author is affiliated with Technogel, the mattress material maker, plus a solid temperature mechanism (Okamoto-Mizuno 2012). A reviewer could fairly choose N. No independent trial of an active cooling pad was found; the Sleepme hot-flash result is a company press release. V3 said the only studies were company-run; that holds for the product. V3's 50 USD a month is too low: Pod 5 hardware runs about 2,849 to 2,999 USD plus Autopilot at 199 to 399 USD a year (third-party pricing pages, searched 2026-10-20), about 135 USD a month over 24 months. Simpler pads cost much less.

items.name: Consistent wake time (±30 min)
items.evidenceFor: feeling more alert in the day
items.evidenceSummary: Large observational studies link steady sleep times to better health. One small student trial found regular times lifted daytime alertness. When weekday sleep runs short, some weekend catch-up can help.
items.humanQuestion: How far does your wake-up time drift on weekends?
items.fitsInstead: Weekend wake-ups within an hour of weekdays, rather than to the minute.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded A from one cohort; regraded B, since the brief's A needs meta-analyses or several RCTs in healthy adults. Evidence: large observational cohorts (Windred 2024: 60,977 people, mean age 63, so not the 22 to 35 group; it measured overall sleep regularity, not wake time alone), a systematic review of mostly observational studies (Chaput 2020, very low to moderate certainty), an expert consensus (Sletten 2023, National Sleep Foundation), one small controlled trial in students (Manber 1996; the abstract does not say whether groups were randomized), and stimulus control, which includes waking at the same time daily, for chronic insomnia (Edinger 2021, conditional, low-quality evidence). No trial isolates wake time alone in healthy adults. V3's '60,000 people' figure is confirmed (60,977). V3's 'single strongest sleep habit we know of' is not something these sources establish. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Screens / phone in bed
items.evidenceFor: winding down and falling asleep
items.evidenceSummary: The research finds no sleep benefit from a phone in bed. In 42 studies of young adults, heavier phone use, especially at night, went with later, shorter, worse sleep. A small trial found a phone-free half hour sped up sleep.
items.humanQuestion: What do you usually do on the phone in bed?
items.originQuestion: How did the phone become part of bedtime?
items.fitsInstead: Charging the phone outside the bedroom, with a book by the bed.
items.notesInternal: The tier grades the benefit people use it for (winding down), which only anecdote supports, so D; the harm evidence lives in the summary. V3 graded the harm as B, which under V4 would add EVIDENCE_REGULAR and protect the habit. Harm evidence is mostly observational (Brautsch 2023: 42 studies, causal direction unclear; Hjetland 2025: cross-sectional, 35% response rate) plus one small pilot RCT with diary-only outcomes (He 2020: 38 students, latency 31 to 18 min vs 29 to 27 min). V3's '20 to 30 minutes later for social media in bed' figure was not confirmed (Levenson 2017 and Exelmans 2016 not opened). Hjetland found no difference between social media and other screen activities, which cuts against V3's 'what you look at matters more than blue light' line; time in bed on the screen seems to matter most.

items.name: Reading (paper) before bed
items.evidenceFor: sleep that feels a little better
items.evidenceSummary: In an online trial of nearly 1,000 adults, a week of reading in bed left 42% reporting better sleep, versus 28% without; sleep was self-rated. A bright tablet disturbed sleep more than paper.
items.humanQuestion: Paper book, e-reader, or tablet?
items.notesInternal: V3 graded C ('small trials versus screens favour paper'); regraded B because two randomized studies agree, though both are short. Finucane 2021 is large (991 randomized) but one week long, unblinded, with a single-item self-reported outcome and more dropouts among readers; e-readers were not excluded and paper was not required. Its secondary sleep-disturbance gain was small. Chang 2015 (12 people, inpatient) compared a printed book with a tablet at full brightness for 4 hours, not with no reading. So the support is for reading in general and for print over bright screens; paper versus e-ink has not been tested. Cost set to 0 because the habit is free; books are optional. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Weekend sleep-in (over 1 h)
items.evidenceFor: making up for short sleep during the week
items.evidenceSummary: Studies disagree. In a Swedish cohort, short weekday sleepers who slept longer on weekends lived as long as steady sleepers, yet a larger device-based study found no benefit. A lab trial found catch-up shifted the body clock later.
items.humanQuestion: Is the lie-in for pleasure, or catching up on short nights?
items.fitsInstead: A lie-in kept under an hour, with an earlier night on Friday.
items.notesInternal: V3 framed it only as harmful (B, social jet lag) and left the goal blank. The evidence conflicts, so C: catch-up looked protective in a Swedish cohort (Akerstedt 2019, self-reported sleep, under-65s only) and in observational studies pooled by Chaput 2020, and the National Sleep Foundation panel endorsed catch-up when weekday sleep is short (Sletten 2023). Against that, device-measured UK Biobank data found no link with mortality or cardiovascular disease (Chaput 2024; per the Gao 2024 editorial, one sensitivity analysis hinted at higher mortality at 2 h or more), and a randomized lab study found weekend recovery delayed the body clock and did not reverse metabolic effects (Depner 2019). Taylor 2008 and Wittmann 2006 could not be opened (no abstract available), so V3's Sunday-night circadian claim rests on Depner here.

items.name: Stretching or yoga before bed
items.evidenceFor: better self-rated sleep quality
items.evidenceSummary: Trials in women with sleep problems found yoga improved self-rated sleep a little. Insomnia scores didn't shift, and bedtime timing itself is barely studied.
studiedForms: mostly in women with sleep problems
items.humanQuestion: Does it help you settle, or feel like homework?
items.fitsInstead: Two minutes of slow breathing in bed keeps the wind-down.
items.notesInternal: Tier C, not B. Wang 2020 (BMC Psychiatry, 19 RCTs, 1832 women with sleep problems): pooled SMD -0.33 overall, PSQI SMD -0.54 across 16 RCTs, but ISI (insomnia) null in 3 RCTs and null in breast-cancer and peri/postmenopausal subgroups. Only women, mostly clinical subgroups, and these were yoga programmes, not specifically bedtime stretching. I found no trial of bedtime stretching in healthy young adults. Free, so no UNUSED. Possible future overlap with wind-down-practices (not added; existing groups can't take new members in this file). V3 note matched roughly.

items.name: Cold shower (morning)
items.evidenceFor: fewer sick days in healthy working adults
items.evidenceSummary: One large Dutch trial found 29% fewer self-reported sick days, though people got ill just as often. Energy wasn't measured.
items.doseTypical: 0.5 to 1.5, at the end of a warm shower
studiedForms: hot shower ending in 30 to 90 seconds of cold water
items.humanQuestion: Is it the wake-up jolt you'd miss?
items.fitsInstead: Thirty cold seconds at the end of a warm shower.
items.notesInternal: Tier C: a single pragmatic RCT (Buijze 2016, PLoS One, n=3018 Dutch workers, opened full text): sickness absence IRR 0.71 at 90 days, illness days unchanged, no difference between 30, 60 and 90 s. Unblinded, all self-report, 20% attrition. Energy was not measured formally; authors only report it as the most common perceived benefit. Cain 2025 meta-analysis (11 studies, mostly baths, only 1 shower) found stress lower at 12 h and an acute inflammation spike, and cites the Buijze sick-day result narratively. Safety row: Buijze excluded people with serious cardiac comorbidity; cold shock is better described for immersion (Shattock 2012) than for showers, so I set clinician-first rather than never-suggest. Free, so no UNUSED. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Trials of cold showers left out people with serious heart conditions, so a clinician is the one to ask first.

items.name: Fitness app subscription (Peloton app, Apple Fitness+, Ladder)
items.evidenceFor: health from regular exercise, when the app's workouts get done
items.evidenceSummary: Regular exercise has strong evidence behind it. The app itself is weaker: in trials, activity apps alone didn't reliably raise daily steps.
items.doseTypical: 150 to 300 moderate, plus strength twice a week
studiedForms: trials tested activity apps against no app
items.humanQuestion: When did you last press play on a workout?
items.notesInternal: Structured like a training row: A for the exercise when it happens (WHO 2020 guidelines, Bull et al., opened abstract: 150-300 min/week moderate plus muscle strengthening), requires trains. tier_otherwise C from Romeo 2019 JMIR (9 RCTs, 1740 adults, objective activity): apps produced a nonsignificant +477 steps/day (P=.19); short programmes under 3 months did better. dose_min 150 min is per week (WHO), not per day; the unit list has no min/week. Price: Apple Fitness+ $9.99/month or $79.99/year (apple.com, opened). Peloton's pricing page rendered $0 (display error), and Ladder wasn't opened, so 15 is an estimate across the three. V3 said B; the 'outlive the habit' line isn't tested for fitness apps specifically (DellaVigna 2006 is gyms). Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Nutrition or calorie app (premium)
items.evidenceFor: small gains in eating habits and weight while logging
items.evidenceSummary: Across 41 studies, app programs that pair logging with coaching brought small gains in eating habits and weight. Logging alone showed no diet change in one trial, and premium tiers are untested.
items.humanQuestion: Do you still log, or just pay?
items.notesInternal: Tier B: Villinger 2019 Obes Rev meta-analysis (41 studies, 27 RCTs, 6348 people): g=0.19 for nutrition behaviours, g=0.30 for obesity indices; commercial vs research app made no difference. Effects are small and the premium tier specifically isn't tested; I wrote the free-tier line from my own knowledge that MyFitnessPal's free tier logs food (not from an opened source) so Veer may want to check. Kept clear_when to UNUSED only so a used app is protected. Safety: Simpson & Mazzeo 2017 (n=493 students, cross-sectional) linked calorie trackers with more eating concern and restraint; Hahn 2021 RCT (200 low-risk undergraduate women, 1 month MyFitnessPal) found no change in eating disorder risk. So the risk sits with people with an eating disorder history; clinician-first. Price: MyFitnessPal Premium $19.99/month or $79.99/year (myfitnesspal.com/premium, opened); annual works out near $7/month. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Calorie logging is linked with more food worry in some people. With an eating disorder history, check with a clinician first.

items.name: Second meditation or sleep app
items.evidenceFor: added benefit from a second app on top of the first
items.evidenceSummary: One mindfulness app gives small lifts in mood and calm in trials. No study has tested whether a second app adds anything.
studiedForms: single mindfulness apps tested against control
items.humanQuestion: Which of the two do you actually open?
items.originQuestion: What got you a second meditation or sleep app?
items.fitsInstead: Keep the one you open most.
items.notesInternal: Tier N for the second app's added value, not for meditation apps generally. Linardon 2024 (45 RCTs) found small effects of one mindfulness app on depression (g=0.24) and anxiety (g=0.28); that protects the first app (separate row). Nothing tests a second app on top. Baumel 2019 (93 Android mental-health apps, independent panel data): median 30-day retention 3.3% overall, 4.7% for mindfulness apps, with morning and night peaks for meditation use (used for moments). Overlap rule keep-most-used handles which one stays. Price is an estimate (Headspace and Calm list roughly $13 to $17/month from my knowledge; their pricing pages failed to load).

items.name: Massage gun (percussive massager)
items.evidenceFor: less stiffness and more flexibility right after use
items.evidenceSummary: Small studies found short-lived gains in flexibility and less stiffness. Strength, speed and jumping didn't improve, and sometimes dipped right after use.
items.humanQuestion: When did it last come out of the case?
items.fitsInstead: A foam roller or tennis ball does a similar job.
items.notesInternal: Tier C: Ferreira 2023 J Funct Morphol Kinesiol systematic review (opened full text, no funding, no COI): 11 studies, 281 mostly young active men, 10 of 11 at moderate risk of bias. Short-term ROM and stiffness gains; no change in lactate or perceived exertion; power, agility and balance null or worse. Long-term effects unknown, and soreness results weren't pooled. Safety row from the review's caution list (DVT, clotting disorders); it also lists pregnancy, pacemakers, recent fractures, which I didn't add as rows. Price: Theragun Prime lists about $299 (TechRadar via search, Therabody page 404'd), spread over 24 months = about $12. Foam-roller swap is my suggestion; not tested head to head here.

safety.note: Skip areas with a known clot or bruise. With a clotting disorder or blood thinners, ask a clinician first.

items.name: Compression boots (Normatec and similar)
items.evidenceFor: less soreness after hard exercise
items.evidenceSummary: A 2024 review of 17 small studies found a small to moderate drop in felt soreness. Effects on strength and damage markers were inconsistent.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the soreness, or the half hour lying still?
items.notesInternal: Tier C: Maia 2024 Biol Sport meta-analysis (opened full text, public grant funding, no COI): 17 studies, 319 athletes and healthy adults. Soreness g=0.49 at 0-2 h and 0.37 at 96 h, nonsignificant at 24-72 h; muscle function trivial and nonsignificant; creatine kinase unclear; lactate and heart rate unaffected. Authors call the evidence preliminary. No safety row added: pneumatic compression is usually avoided with a suspected clot, but neither the review nor the Hyperice page I opened says so, so I left it out; worth Veer adding with a source. Price: Normatec 3 Legs $899 (hyperice.com, opened), /24 = about $37; Normatec Go $379, Elite Legs $1,099. Legs-up swap is my suggestion, untested. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Vibration plate
items.evidenceFor: fat loss and body shape in younger adults
items.evidenceSummary: In trials of heavier adults, fat loss averaged about one kilo, too small to matter. Bone gains show up mainly in women over 60.
studiedForms: standing or squatting on a platform
items.humanQuestion: What were you hoping it would change?
items.fitsInstead: Ten minutes of squats and heel raises, no plate.
items.notesInternal: Tier C for the outcome 22-35s buy it for. Rubio-Arias 2021 Arch Phys Med Rehabil (23 studies, 884 overweight or obese, mostly women; abstract): fat mass -1.07 kg, called not clinically significant; also lower systolic BP (-7 mmHg) and better leg strength, which is a real but separate effect. Reis-Silva 2023 Front Physiol (8 RCTs, over-60s; abstract): no body-composition change. Chen 2026 BMC Musculoskelet Disord (14 RCTs, 1447 adults 60-93, 96% women; opened full text): small BMD gains at hip sub-sites, high GRADE; doesn't carry to young adults. Chen notes high-intensity vibration may cause dizziness and falls; no safety row added. Price is an estimate: home plates sell for roughly $100 to $300, spread over 24 months.

items.name: Jaw exerciser (jawline trainer)
items.evidenceFor: a more defined jawline
items.evidenceSummary: No trials. In a 2024 two-person report, three months of use changed nothing visible. Chewing muscles don't shape the fat or skin under the chin.
items.humanQuestion: Has your jaw felt sore since starting?
items.originQuestion: Where did you first see the jaw exerciser?
items.notesInternal: Tier N: no controlled studies. Verma 2024 Cureus (opened full text, no funding) is a two-case report where the subjects were also authors: about 3 months, 10-min sessions 1-3x/week, no change in jawline or double chin; complaints were gagging and suction, no TMJ pain reported. Its literature section says masticatory muscles don't act on submental fat. For TMJ risk I found no dental-association statement on jaw exercisers; nearest is Alam 2025 systematic review on gum chewing (8 studies, mixed: some show dose-related muscle discomfort, others no link). So the safety row is a gentle note, not never-suggest. Area set to skin since it is bought for looks. Price: about $10 per Verma; spread to $3/month as an estimate (cheap, often replaced).

safety.note: If your jaw clicks, locks or aches, a dentist is the one to ask before any jaw training.

items.name: EMF blockers and anti-radiation phone stickers
items.evidenceFor: lower exposure or better health
items.evidenceSummary: No evidence these reduce exposure. The FTC charged sellers over false claims, and lab tests found no drop. The FDA links no health problem to phone signals.
studiedForms: phone stickers and patches (independent tests only)
items.humanQuestion: What made the phone start to feel worrying?
items.originQuestion: Where did you hear about EMF stickers?
items.fitsInstead: Phone across the room at night keeps the calm.

swap.title: Phone across the room at night

items.notesInternal: Tier N. FTC press release 20 Feb 2002 (opened): charged SV1 and Comstar (WaveShield) over claims of blocking 97-99% of radiation; quotes Good Housekeeping Institute tests showing no reduction and an FTC consumer alert saying no proof shields reduce exposure; also notes most emission comes from the antenna, not the earpiece. FDA page (current as of 13 May 2021, opened): weight of evidence has not linked phone RF with health problems; page says nothing about shields. Newer wearable 'EMF' pendants weren't checked separately. Price: one-off purchase, roughly $20 to $40 (estimate), spread to about $2/month. Phone-across-the-room swap is my own suggestion.

items.name: Unlisted subscription you're still paying for
items.evidenceFor: any wellness benefit while it sits unused
items.evidenceSummary: A subscription only helps when it gets used. A large gym study found members often paid for far more than got used.
items.humanQuestion: Do you remember signing up for this?
items.originQuestion: Do you remember how this subscription started?
items.notesInternal: Catch-all row for any subscription a person forgot about; kept general as asked: tier N, clear_when UNUSED only (no BORROWED_WEAK, since the engine shouldn't judge an unknown product's evidence). Area 'mind' is a placeholder; the schema needs one, and Veer may want a neutral option. Cost 0 because the real amount comes from the person's own statement. DellaVigna 2006 AER (opened abstract): monthly gym members paid over $70 for 4.3 visits a month, over $17 a visit vs $10 on a pass, overestimated future attendance and delayed cancelling. It's gyms only, so I used it for the general pattern, not a tier. V3's '30 days unused' threshold has no source I found; it's a product rule. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Eye mask
items.evidenceFor: sleep and next-day alertness when light reaches the bed
items.evidenceSummary: In young adults, a week of sleeping in a mask gave a small lift in next-day memory and reaction time. In bright hospital rooms, masks improved sleep.
studiedForms: contoured or flat blackout eye mask
items.humanQuestion: Does light get into your room at night?
items.notesInternal: Tier B, not A: Greco 2023 (Sleep, ERC-funded, no conflicts) ran two counterbalanced within-subject experiments in 18-35s (n=89 and 33); mask vs no/holed mask gave small gains in word-pair learning (d about 0.19) and PVT reaction time (d 0.16), but self-rated sleepiness and Dreem-measured sleep stages did not differ, and allocation was counterbalanced, not described as randomised. Karimi 2021 meta (35 studies, mostly ICU patients) found masks and/or earplugs improved sleep quality; eye-mask-only studies mostly positive but heterogeneous, no GRADE. Hu 2010: 14 healthy volunteers in recorded ICU noise and 100 lux light; masks plus earplugs gave more REM and fewer arousals (combined, so mask effect not isolated). Consistent direction, small and narrow samples, hence B. Price: estimate, a $10-20 mask lasting about a year. wearable_sees partial: wearables can see sleep but not the mask.

items.name: Earplugs
items.evidenceFor: sleep in a noisy room
items.evidenceSummary: In a lab night of loud recorded hospital noise, earplugs with a mask gave more dream sleep and fewer brief wakings. Most other studies are in hospital patients.
items.humanQuestion: Is your room noisy at night?
items.notesInternal: Tier B kept from V3 but scoped to noisy rooms. Hu 2010 (Crit Care, n=14 healthy volunteers, randomised night order, about 66 dB(A) playback): plugs plus mask raised REM 9.3% to 12.9%, cut arousal index 15.1 to 12.2, better perceived sleep; total sleep time and sleep latency not significant; plugs and mask combined. Karimi 2021 meta: earplug-only ICU studies mixed (Litton 2017, Baghaie Lakeh 2018 null). No good trial in quiet bedrooms or of healthy people at home, so evidence_for is limited to noise. I did not find a review of earplugs in healthy adults at home. Price: estimate, foam plugs about $0.10-0.20 a pair, reusable silicone/Loop-style a one-off $25-35. In noise-masking group with white noise (show-together, not redundancy, so no OVERLAP clear code here). Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: White noise / sound machine
items.evidenceFor: falling asleep faster and sleeping more soundly
items.evidenceSummary: A 2021 review of 38 studies rated the evidence very low. Some found falling asleep faster, and at least one found more broken sleep.
items.humanQuestion: Is there noise to cover, or is it the sound?
items.fitsInstead: A sound app or a fan gives the same steady sound.
items.notesInternal: Riedy 2021 (Sleep Med Rev 55:101385, PROSPERO-registered, 38 studies): GRADE very low for continuous noise improving sleep; findings ranged from improved to disrupted; authors warn about possible harm to sleep and hearing and call for objective measures. Read abstract via Europe PMC only (PubMed blocked). C not D because there are many human studies, just inconsistent. The V3 line about masking real noise is plausible but I did not find a trial isolating it. Price: estimate, $30-60 machine over 24 months, apps often free. OVERLAP code is there for people who use both earplugs and a machine; Veer may prefer to drop it. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Keep the volume low and the speaker away from your head. Loud all-night sound may affect hearing.

items.name: Sunrise alarm (Hatch and similar)
items.evidenceFor: feeling more alert on waking
items.evidenceSummary: Small trials, one with eight people, found waking to slowly brightening light felt more alert and gave slightly quicker reactions. Larger trials are missing.
items.doseTypical: light rising over the last 30 minutes before waking
studiedForms: dawn simulator lamp ramping up before alarm
items.humanQuestion: Do you wake easier with it than without?
items.fitsInstead: Open curtains and a short walk outside bring real morning light.
items.notesInternal: Thompson 2014 (Eur J Appl Physiol 114:1049, n=8 people who find waking hard, random-order crossover): dawn light in last 30 min raised self-rated sleep quality and alertness, more additions and faster reaction time; cycling time trial not significant. Abstract only. Golden 2005 meta: dawn simulation for seasonal depression effect size 0.73 from 5 studies (abstract) - a different outcome, noted for context only. Search also surfaced Gabel 2013 (n=17, sleep restriction) which I did not open. Small and few, hence C. Price: hatch.co Restore 3 page lists $169.99 (opened 2026-10-22) = about $7/month over 24 months; Hatch+ subscription price not shown on page, so 8 is an estimate. moments includes night because Hatch-type devices also run wind-down sounds/light.

items.name: Blue-light blocking glasses
items.evidenceFor: better sleep quality
items.evidenceSummary: A 2023 Cochrane review found six small trials on sleep: three showed better sleep, three showed no difference. Certainty was rated very low.
items.humanQuestion: Do evenings feel calmer with them on?
items.fitsInstead: Dimmer lamps and lower screen brightness after dark keep the wind-down.
items.notesInternal: Singh 2023 Cochrane CD013244 (17 trials total; 6 RCTs, 148 people, for sleep): 3 positive, 3 null, no meta-analysis possible, very low certainty. Cochrane full text returned 403; read abstract via Europe PMC. Reported adverse effects included headache, discomfort and lower mood. C (studies disagree) rather than D. Note the V3 claim that the review 'pooled all trials and found little effect' was inaccurate: it could not pool sleep data. The cheaper alternative leans on general evening-light evidence (existing chang-2015-ereader-sleep) rather than a glasses source. Price: estimate, $20-60 glasses over 24 months.

items.name: Nasal strips or dilators
items.evidenceFor: less snoring and easier nose breathing at night
items.evidenceSummary: Strips and dilators open the nose a little. A 2016 review of people with sleep apnea found no measurable drop in snoring or apnea.
studiedForms: external strips (Breathe Right) and internal dilators (Nozovent)
items.humanQuestion: Is it a stuffy nose or loud snoring?
items.notesInternal: Camacho 2016 (Pulm Med, 14 studies, 294 patients, mostly small non-randomised, people with snoring/OSA): snore index change not significant (-2.5/hr overall; strips -3.1/hr), AHI unchanged, lowest O2 sat +1% (abstract and results disagree on significance). One included study found bed partners reported mildly less snoring. Improved nasal airflow is accepted. A consumer site claimed two GSK-sponsored RCTs found no sleep-quality benefit vs placebo strips; I could not verify, not used. C rather than D because human trials exist with mixed subjective vs objective results. Price: estimate, about $0.40-0.50 per strip nightly. Safety row added for sleep apnea. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Strips don't change sleep apnea. Loud snoring with gasping or heavy daytime sleepiness is worth a clinician visit.

items.name: Silk pillowcase
items.evidenceFor: smoother hair and fewer breakouts
items.evidenceSummary: No trials of real silk on hair or skin. One small trial of a silk-like pillowcase found no fewer breakouts than cotton. Less friction on hair is plausible but untested.
items.humanQuestion: Is it for your hair, your skin, or the feel?
items.originQuestion: What first sold you on a silk pillowcase?
items.fitsInstead: A satin pillowcase gives the same smooth feel.
items.notesInternal: D: for hair the only support is friction reasoning and a seller's own lab test (Mulberry Park Silks, not opened, brand). The one registered trial (NCT00767104, Wake Forest, collaborator Precision Fabrics Group, n=40, 12 weeks, results posted 2017) used a silk-like synthetic, not silk, and found 13% vs 22% lesion reduction for silk-like vs cotton with overlapping CIs - no benefit. Healthline's claim that this trial showed fewer pimples contradicts the posted results. Marked brand_funded yes because a fabric maker collaborated (funding split not stated). Price: estimate, $25-90 pillowcase over 24 months. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Weighted blanket
items.evidenceFor: easing insomnia in adults
items.evidenceSummary: One strong trial in people with insomnia plus anxiety, depression, ADHD or bipolar found large gains. Pooled with other trials, the sleep effect was not clear.
items.doseTypical: 6 to 8 kg blanket in the main trial
studiedForms: weighted chain blanket vs light control blanket
items.humanQuestion: Do you fall asleep easier under it?
items.notesInternal: Downgraded V3 B to C; Veer may want B scoped to people with insomnia plus a mental health condition. Ekholm 2020 (JCSM, n=120 psychiatric outpatients with insomnia, 4 weeks, blinded raters, Region Stockholm funded, no COI): ISI response 59% vs 5%, remission 42% vs 4%; actigraphy total sleep time and WASO unchanged; blinding of participants weak (weight is obvious). Zhao 2024 meta (8 RCTs, 426 psychiatric patients, about half high risk of bias): pooled insomnia MD -1.92 ISI, p=0.06 (significant only after dropping one study); anxiety small benefit. No trial in healthy 22-35s found. Self-reported benefit outruns objective change. Price: estimate, $60-150 over 24 months. Safety row for babies/children (CPSC). dose_unit left blank because kg is not an allowed unit.

safety.note: Weighted blankets are not safe for babies. For a child, a pediatrician is the first stop.

items.name: Light therapy box (10,000 lux)
items.evidenceFor: easing low mood in winter (seasonal depression)
items.evidenceSummary: In people diagnosed with seasonal depression, a 2020 review of 19 trials found bright light eased winter low mood more than dim light. For ordinary winter blues it is untested.
items.humanQuestion: Are winter mornings the hard part?
items.fitsInstead: A morning walk outside brings bright light too, though it hasn't been tested the same way.
items.notesInternal: B: Pjrek 2020 (Psychother Psychosom, 19 RCTs vs dim light or sham ion generators): depression SMD -0.37, response RR 1.42, no publication bias, but moderate heterogeneity and moderate-high risk of bias (abstract). Golden 2005 meta: bright light ES 0.84 for seasonal depression, 0.53 non-seasonal (abstract). Not A: population is people with SAD, not healthy adults; evidence_requires has no 'seasonal low mood' option, so it is in evidence_for. For people without winter low mood the benefit is unproven; the engine may want a seasonal flag. Dose: 20-30 min at 10,000 lux each morning is the standard clinical protocol, but I did not open a dosing source, so dose_min is blank. Safety: Takeshima 2020 meta (6 RCTs, bipolar depression) found switch rate 4.7%, similar to control, mostly with mood stabilisers; authors suspect higher risk without one - kept clinician-first for bipolar. Price: estimate, $40-100 box over 24 months. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: With bipolar disorder, bright light can tip mood upward. Worth starting with a clinician, ideally alongside existing care.

items.name: Grounding or earthing (sheets, mats)
items.evidenceFor: better sleep
items.evidenceSummary: Most studies are tiny and run by people tied to grounding companies. One small independent trial, in older adults with Alzheimer's, found better sleep scores.
studiedForms: conductive mattress pad or mat wired to ground
items.humanQuestion: Do you sleep differently with it or without?
items.originQuestion: Where did you come across grounding?
items.fitsInstead: Barefoot time on grass or sand keeps the outdoor part.

swap.title: Barefoot time on grass or sand

items.notesInternal: Chevalier 2012 review: three of five authors are contractors for and shareholders in the earthing company; the sleep study (Ghaly and Teplitz 2004, n=12) had no control group. That evidence counts as brand. Lin 2022 (Healthcare, n=22 randomised, 15 completed, mild Alzheimer's, age about 78, no funding, no COI declared, used an Earthing-brand mat): PSQI better vs sham at week 12 (p=0.006) but GEE model p=0.053; later corrected. A Korean pilot (n=60) surfaced in search but I did not open it. Grade D not N because one independent pilot exists, but it is tiny and in a very different population; no plausible mechanism shown. Price: estimate, $50-150 over 24 months; V3 had 30, which looks high. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Salt lamp
items.evidenceFor: cleaner air, better mood or sleep
items.evidenceSummary: No studies. Clinicians note the lamps give off too few ions to change the air, mood or sleep. The warm glow is the real part.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the warm glow you like?
items.originQuestion: How did the salt lamp end up in your room?
items.fitsInstead: Any warm, dim lamp gives the same evening glow.

swap.title: A warm, dim lamp in the evening

items.notesInternal: N: no peer-reviewed study of salt lamps on air, mood or sleep found. Cleveland Clinic (2021, Neha Vyas MD) says output is too low to matter and benefits are anecdotal. Healthline cites a Negative Ion Information Center test showing barely measurable ions; not opened or verified. Note: 'treat' in why_loved is the allowed code, not person-facing text. Price: estimate, $15-30 lamp over 24 months; V3 had 0. Kind set to environment since it is room decor.

items.name: Probiotic (generic daily capsule)
items.evidenceFor: better gut health and digestion in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: Benefits depend on the exact strain and the problem. In healthy adults, trials found brief shifts in gut bacteria and some help with regularity, but little lasting change.
items.doseTypical: one capsule, often 1 to 50 billion CFU
studiedForms: results do not carry across strains
items.humanQuestion: Did a clinician suggest a strain for something specific?
items.fitsInstead: Yogurt or kefir with breakfast keeps the habit.
items.notesInternal: Tier C, kept from V3. Khalesi 2019 (45 trials, healthy adults) found transient colonisation and some support for stool consistency, bowel movements and immune markers; no persistent microbiome change. Rauch 2022 found no improvement in gut symptoms or permeability in healthy or active adults. Strain-specific evidence (e.g. antibiotic-associated diarrhoea) does not transfer to a generic daily capsule; I could not open the AGA 2020 guideline full text (403), so it is not cited. If someone was prescribed a strain for a diagnosed condition, that falls outside this row. Price: $30/month is the V3 estimate, not checked against a pricing page. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: With serious illness or a weakened immune system, probiotics carry more risk. Check with a clinician first.

items.name: Zinc (daily supplement)
items.evidenceFor: catching fewer colds from taking zinc every day
items.evidenceSummary: A 2024 Cochrane review found daily zinc made little difference to how often people caught colds. Zinc started once a cold begins may shorten it, though the evidence is weak.
studiedForms: zinc gluconate or acetate lozenges for colds
items.humanQuestion: Do you take it daily, or only with colds?
items.fitsInstead: Zinc lozenges at the first sign of a cold, instead of daily.
items.notesInternal: Tier C rather than D: Cochrane 2024 (34 RCTs) gives prevention RR 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01), low certainty, so a small effect is not ruled out. Treatment use (lozenges once a cold starts) may cut about 2.4 days, low certainty, high heterogeneity; Hemila has published critiques of this review arguing the lozenge effect is understated (not opened, titles only). V3's 'does nothing when not low' is roughly right for prevention. Upper limit 40 mg/day is set to avoid copper deficiency (LPI). Most daily multivitamins already carry zinc, hence the overlap. Price is the V3 estimate.

safety.note: Above 40 mg a day of zinc, from all sources, can lower copper over time. A multivitamin may already include zinc.
Zinc can reduce absorption of some antibiotics. Spacing the two at least two hours apart usually helps.

items.name: Vitamin C (daily supplement)
items.evidenceFor: slightly shorter colds in adults who take it every day
items.evidenceSummary: Across about 30 placebo trials, daily vitamin C did not cut how often adults caught colds, but made colds about 8% shorter. Cheap and well tolerated.
studiedForms: ascorbic acid tablets taken daily (starting at a cold showed no consistent effect)
items.humanQuestion: Is this mostly for cold season?
items.fitsInstead: An orange or kiwi keeps the morning habit, though at less than the 200 mg studied.
items.notesInternal: Tier A for the narrow claim only: Cochrane 2013, 31 comparisons, 9,745 episodes; duration down 8% (3 to 12%) in adults, 14% in children. Incidence RR 0.97 in the general community; RR 0.48 in marathon runners, skiers and soldiers under heavy physical stress (could justify a stronger keep for heavy endurance trainers). Starting vitamin C once a cold begins showed no consistent effect, so the benefit needs regular daily use. dose_min 200 mg is the review's inclusion floor. LPI: full absorption up to 200 mg per dose, plasma plateaus at 200 to 400 mg/day, so 1,000 mg adds little. The effect is small; the A is about how solid the evidence is, not its size. Price is the V3 estimate. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: High-dose vitamin C raises urine oxalate. With kidney stones or kidney disease, 1 g a day or more is worth checking first.

items.name: Iron supplement
items.evidenceFor: less tiredness and restored iron stores in adults with low iron
items.evidenceSummary: When iron is low, even without anaemia, trials found iron eased tiredness and rebuilt iron stores. With normal iron, no benefit is shown, and extra iron can build up.
items.doseTypical: 60 mg elemental iron, often on alternate mornings, or as prescribed
studiedForms: ferrous sulfate and other oral iron salts
items.humanQuestion: Has a blood test shown your iron is low?
items.notesInternal: Tier A with deficiency: Houston 2018 BMJ Open, 18 RCTs, fatigue SMD -0.38 (4 trials, 714) in iron-deficient non-anaemic adults; no gain in measured VO2max. Treating iron-deficiency anaemia is standard care. tier_otherwise D: I found no trial benefit in iron-replete adults, and LPI advises against iron without evaluation for people not at risk and for haemochromatosis. dose_min 60 mg is taken from Stoffel 2017 (60 mg morning doses on alternate days absorbed best in iron-depleted women); real dosing belongs to the clinician, so I did not add DOSE_BELOW_MIN. LPI upper limit 45 mg/day applies to unsupervised use. At-risk groups per LPI: menstruating women, endurance athletes, vegetarians and vegans, frequent blood donors. Cadence is daily in the table but alternate-day is common. Price is the V3 estimate.

safety.note: Iron is best started after a blood test shows low iron. Extra iron when levels are normal can build up and cause harm.
Iron can weaken thyroid medicine, some antibiotics and other drugs. Spacing the two about two hours apart usually helps.

items.name: Vitamin B12
items.evidenceFor: healthy B12 levels for vegans and people who eat little animal food
items.evidenceSummary: Vegans often run low, and a small daily B12 restores healthy levels. In people with enough B12, trials found no benefit for mood or memory.
items.humanQuestion: Do you eat little meat, fish, eggs or dairy?
items.fitsInstead: A fortified plant milk or cereal can cover the daily amount.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded N; that was wrong. For vegans the need is well established: Niklewicz 2024 meta-analysis shows lower B12 and higher homocysteine in vegans, with supplement users better on every marker; Del Bo 2019 RCT (40 vegans/vegetarians, marginal deficiency) restored levels with about 50 mcg/day. Graded B, not A, because the RCT evidence is small and status-based; correcting deficiency itself is standard care. I used low_intake (vegan/low animal food); people with a measured low level, metformin users and acid-reducer users are also at risk (LPI) and should also be protected; the engine may want deficiency too. tier_otherwise D: Markun 2021 (16 RCTs, 6,276) found no effect on cognition or depression without overt deficiency; fatigue was measured in only one trial, so 'no energy benefit' is inferred, not proven. LPI: only 1 to 2% of large oral doses absorbed, no upper limit. Price is the V3 estimate.

safety.note: Metformin and stomach-acid medicines can lower B12 over time. A B12 test is worth asking about.

items.name: Turmeric or curcumin supplement
items.evidenceFor: less joint pain and soreness in active, healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: Trials in older adults with knee arthritis found less pain with curcumin extracts. Small trials hint at less soreness after hard exercise. Plain turmeric powder is poorly absorbed.
studiedForms: often with piperine or absorption-enhanced forms
items.humanQuestion: Is it for sore joints, or general wellness?
items.fitsInstead: Turmeric in cooking, with black pepper, keeps the ritual.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded B on knee arthritis. The arthritis evidence is real (Zeng 2021: 15 RCTs, 1,621; NCCIH calls it positive but needing higher quality), but it comes from older adults with osteoarthritis, not the 22 to 35 audience, and many trials carry bias risk. For what this audience buys it for (soreness, general inflammation), Fang 2021 pooled small trials with modest gains in soreness and CK; earlier trials were inconsistent. So C for evidence_for. If someone has diagnosed knee arthritis, B would fit; no evidence_requires code covers that. FORM_NOT_ABSORBED: Anand 2007 and LPI on low bioavailability; plain powder capsules are the target. Safety: DILIN 2023 liver-injury cases (often with piperine), NCCIH says highly bioavailable products have been linked to liver damage, LPI notes antiplatelet effects. V3's gallstone caution: LPI notes increased gallbladder contraction only; no gallstone source opened, so not added. Price is the V3 estimate.

safety.note: Concentrated turmeric and curcumin products have been linked to liver injury. Check with a clinician first.
Curcumin can slow blood clotting. With blood thinners such as warfarin, aspirin or clopidogrel, check with a clinician first.
Turmeric in food is fine, but turmeric supplements may be unsafe in pregnancy.
Stop and see a clinician with tiredness, nausea, dark urine or yellowing skin or eyes.

items.name: Psyllium husk or fibre supplement
items.evidenceFor: more regular bowel movements and lower LDL cholesterol when fibre intake is low
items.evidenceSummary: About 10 g a day lowered LDL cholesterol across 28 trials. In adults with constipation, psyllium made bowel movements more regular, best above 10 g daily for four weeks.
items.doseTypical: about 10, often split across the day
studiedForms: psyllium husk powder or capsules (Plantago ovata)
items.humanQuestion: Does it keep things regular for you?
items.fitsInstead: Oats, beans and berries add fibre too.
items.notesInternal: Tier A: Jovanovski 2018 (28 RCTs, 1,924) LDL -0.33 mmol/L at a median 10.2 g/day, moderate-quality GRADE, in people with or without high cholesterol; van der Schoot 2022 (16 RCTs, 1,251, chronic constipation) responder rate 66% vs 41%, psyllium strongest, best above 10 g/day for 4+ weeks. evidence_requires low_intake as Veer asked, since the regularity benefit was shown in people with constipation. tier_otherwise B rather than lower because the LDL effect held regardless of baseline cholesterol, which suggests it does not depend on a low-fibre diet. dose_min 10 g comes from both reviews; many people take one teaspoon (about 5 g), which DOSE_BELOW_MIN would flag. The suggestion there should be 'a little more', not 'let it go'. More wind is the common side effect. No safety row: I did not open a source on spacing it from medicines. Price $12 is an estimate (V3 said $10).

items.name: Krill oil
items.evidenceFor: heart health in people who rarely eat oily fish
items.evidenceSummary: Krill oil carries the same omega-3 fats as fish oil and lowers blood fats the same per gram. Most capsules hold far less omega-3 than heart trials used.
items.doseTypical: about 100 to 250 EPA plus DHA per capsule
studiedForms: krill oil softgels (EPA + DHA as phospholipids)
items.humanQuestion: How often do you eat oily fish?
items.fitsInstead: Oily fish twice a week, or a standard fish oil.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded B; I matched the reviewed omega-3-fish-oil row (C, low_intake, otherwise D, dose_min 840 mg EPA+DHA from VITAL), since krill's benefit is its omega-3. Kim 2020 network meta-analysis (64 RCTs): no difference from fish oil on lipids; effect tracks n-3 dose. Laslett 2024 JAMA: 2 g/day krill oil did not help knee osteoarthritis pain. Label checked: NOW Neptune Krill 1000 mg = 120 EPA + 70 DHA (190 mg) per softgel, so one capsule is about a quarter of the VITAL dose; MegaRed's site did not show EPA/DHA in text. Krill bioavailability claims (e.g. Ramprasath 2013, omega-3 index) exist but co-authors appear industry-linked; not cited. No krill-specific safety row: fish oil's bleeding and blood-thinner rows likely apply, but I opened no krill source. Price $30 is the V3 estimate.

items.name: CoQ10 (coenzyme Q10)
items.evidenceFor: more energy and less fatigue in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: For energy and exercise in healthy adults, trials find small, inconsistent effects. For muscle aches from statins, reviews disagree, and NIH finds the evidence unconvincing.
items.humanQuestion: Are you on a statin, or taking it for energy?
items.notesInternal: Tier C. Energy: Tsai 2022 (13 RCTs, 1,126) found reduced fatigue including healthy participants, but Deng 2025 (24 trials, healthy adults) found small, unstable effects on performance, very low to low certainty, with fatigue only suggestive. So V3's 'does nothing for energy' overstates it; 'small and inconsistent' is fair. Statin myalgia: Qu 2018 positive (12 RCTs), Kennedy 2020 null (7 RCTs), Kovacic 2025 small positive (7 RCTs); NCCIH says overall evidence does not support it. Someone on a statin who feels it helps should be handled gently. Warfarin interaction per NCCIH (safety row). Price $25 is the V3 estimate.

safety.note: CoQ10 may interact with warfarin. Check with a prescriber first.

items.name: Evening primrose oil
items.evidenceFor: calmer eczema or easier PMS
items.evidenceSummary: Careful reviews found evening primrose oil works no better than a placebo for eczema. For PMS, the few trials are small, and the best-run ones found no benefit.
items.humanQuestion: What did you start it for?
items.originQuestion: Who first suggested evening primrose oil?
items.notesInternal: V3 graded N, but independent trials exist and found no benefit, so D fits the table's practice for tested-and-null items (as with phone-in-bed). Bamford 2013 Cochrane (19 EPO trials) found no improvement in eczema and called further trials hard to justify; the lead author had past Efamol trial support, but the review was independent. PMS: Budeiri 1996 (7 trials) found the two best-controlled showed no benefit; NCCIH 2024 calls PMS and menopause evidence insufficient and breast pain probably no better than placebo. V3's 'Whelan 2009' was not found; not cited. Area set to skin because eczema is the main claim. dose_typical 1 to 3 g is a common label range, not checked against trials. Bamford notes a possible bleeding interaction with warfarin. Price is the V3 estimate.

safety.note: Evening primrose oil may raise bleeding with warfarin. Check with a prescriber first.

items.name: Acupuncture
items.evidenceFor: relief from chronic pain (back, neck, knee arthritis, headache)
items.evidenceSummary: In people with chronic pain, 39 trials found acupuncture eased pain more than sham needling or none, mostly lasting a year. The gain over sham is small, and other uses are untested.
studiedForms: needle acupuncture vs sham or no acupuncture
items.humanQuestion: Is it for pain, or for the calm?
items.notesInternal: Tier B for chronic pain only: Vickers 2018 IPD meta-analysis (39 high-quality trials, 20,827 patients) beat sham (~0.2 SD) and no acupuncture (~0.5 SD); NCCIH 2022 agrees, cites ACP 2017 and ACR 2019 guidelines. Effect over sham is small, so B not A. Area set to mind because most 22-35 users go for stress/calm; for stress, sleep or general wellness without pain I did not open trials and V3 called sleep trials weak, so treat non-pain use as C/D in conversation (human_question separates the two). B keep applies on paper to everyone; if the engine can key on purpose, only protect for pain. Safety: NCCIH says serious harms are rare and tied to non-sterile needles or untrained practitioners; no specific condition row sourced (bleeding-risk caution is common practice but I did not open a source, so no row). Cost: estimate, about $100-130 a session, roughly one a week or less; no pricing page opened. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Chiropractor (maintenance visits)
items.evidenceFor: fewer back pain days in people with recurring low back pain
items.evidenceSummary: For chronic low back pain, manipulation works about as well as other recommended care. One trial found planned visits meant fewer pain days for people whose pain kept returning.
studiedForms: scheduled visits after a good first response
items.humanQuestion: Does your back still flare up between visits?
items.fitsInstead: A short daily back routine, and a visit when it flares.
items.notesInternal: Graded C on purpose. Rubinstein 2019 BMJ (47 RCTs, 9,211 adults): SMT similar to other recommended therapies for chronic LBP (moderate quality); two authors were chiropractors with chiropractic-association grants (flagged; brand_funded set no because not a product brand). Eklund 2018 PLoS One pragmatic RCT (n=328, no competing interests): maintenance care gave 12.8 fewer bothersome-pain days over a year vs symptom-guided care, but only in people with recurrent/persistent LBP who responded well to initial care, at ~1.7 more visits. For pain-free 'maintenance' I found no trials (effectively N). V3's claim that maintenance has no evidence was too strong for people with recurring pain, so I did not grade D/N; C lets their values decide and the question surfaces whether pain recurs. If Veer prefers, this could be B with an evidence_requires value for 'recurring back pain' if one is ever added. Cost: estimate ~$65 a visit, about monthly; no pricing page opened. No safety row: Rubinstein found mostly mild transient musculoskeletal events; I did not open sources on neck manipulation and artery injury.

items.name: Hormone or peptide clinic (TRT, GLP-1, peptides)
items.evidenceFor: weight loss with prescribed GLP-1 drugs in adults with obesity
items.evidenceSummary: For adults with obesity, prescribed GLP-1 drugs lower weight well; testosterone helps men with confirmed low levels. Injectable wellness peptides and compounded copies have little safety data.
studiedForms: semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly and other GLP-1 drugs
items.humanQuestion: Who checks your labs and doses?
items.notesInternal: never_clear yes per brief: prescribing care is the clinician's call, Distill only adds safety framing. Tier A applies to the GLP-1 part: Shi 2024 Lancet NMA (republished after 2022 retraction; 132 RCTs, 48,209 adults; independent funding) GLP-1 RAs ~5.8% extra weight loss, semaglutide ~11.4%; STEP 1 (Novo-funded) -14.9% vs -2.4%. TRT: Endocrine Society 2018 says diagnose only with symptoms plus repeatedly low morning T, and lists contraindications (planning fertility, prostate/breast cancer, high hematocrit, untreated severe OSA, uncontrolled heart failure, recent MI/stroke). Peptides (BPC-157, TB-500, CJC-1295, ipamorelin etc.): FDA compounding page (current 2026-04-22) lists them as withdrawn nominations or Category 2 with little or no human safety data: effectively tier N/D. FDA GLP-1 page (current 2026-10-01): compounded semaglutide/tirzepatide not FDA-reviewed, dosing-error hospitalisations, salt forms unlawful, counterfeit risk, 990+ and 730+ adverse event reports. Cadence weekly = typical weekly injection; moments any. Cost $300 is V3 estimate (telehealth GLP-1 programmes and TRT clinics vary roughly $150-1,300); no pricing page opened. area eat chosen since GLP-1 weight programmes dominate in this age group; TRT is move/energy. wearable_sees partial: resting HR and weight trends only. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Hormones, GLP-1s and peptides belong with a licensed prescriber, lab checks and an FDA-approved or state-licensed pharmacy source. Skip anything sold for research use.
Testosterone is not started after a recent heart attack or stroke, or with uncontrolled heart failure. A cardiologist and endocrinologist decide together.
Testosterone is not started while severe sleep apnea goes unmanaged. Getting the apnea looked after comes first.

items.name: CBT-I with a sleep clinician or trained coach
items.evidenceFor: falling asleep faster and waking less in adults with chronic insomnia
items.evidenceSummary: CBT-I is the first-choice approach for chronic insomnia. In 20 trials of people with insomnia, sleep came about 19 minutes sooner with 26 fewer minutes awake, and the gains seemed to last.
items.humanQuestion: Is the sleep window getting easier to keep?
items.notesInternal: Tier A: Trauer 2015 Ann Intern Med meta-analysis (20 RCTs, 1,162 adults with chronic insomnia, no funding): SOL -19 min, WASO -26 min, SE +9.9%, sustained; TST only +7.6 min (CI crosses 0). AASM 2021 guideline: STRONG recommendation for multicomponent CBT-I. Population is people with chronic insomnia, not all healthy adults, but evidence_for names that group. never_clear yes because a trained CBT-I clinician is sleep care; caution: 'sleep coach' is unregulated and many coaches do not deliver CBT-I (stimulus control plus sleep restriction plus cognitive work). Name says 'trained coach' to signal that; if Veer wants untrained sleep coaching as a separate row it should be C/N and clearable. I left fits_instead empty to avoid steering people away from clinician care; a possible line is the free VA 'CBT-i Coach' app, but I did not open a source for it. dose_typical from common practice (Trauer required >=3 components but I did not read session counts in the abstract), so dose_min left blank. Cost $200/month is V3 estimate; no pricing page opened. wearable_sees partial: bed and wake times are visible. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Nutritionist or registered dietitian
items.evidenceFor: better diet quality, weight and blood sugar
items.evidenceSummary: In primary-care patients, one-to-one dietitian visits improved diet quality and, for people with diabetes, blood sugar. Extra weight loss was modest, about 1 kg.
studiedForms: one-to-one dietitian consultations in primary care
items.humanQuestion: Has anything on your plate changed since starting?
items.notesInternal: Tier B: Mitchell 2017 J Acad Nutr Diet systematic review (26 RCTs, 5,500 adults) favoured dietitian consults for glycaemic control (4/4), dietary change (4/4) and anthropometry; not lipids or BP. Williams 2019 meta-analysis (5 RCTs, n=1,598): -1.03 kg extra weight, risk of bias unclear to high, so B not A. Evidence is for registered dietitians; 'nutritionist' is not a protected title in most US states, so a non-credentialed nutritionist or health coach is closer to C/N. Not never_clear (not prescribing care) but if it is for diabetes, kidney disease or an eating disorder it is part of medical care: the engine should not suggest letting go then (no safety row because I did not open a source specific to that). Cost: estimate ~$150 for a monthly follow-up visit (V3 had 200); no pricing page opened. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Blood panel subscription (Function and similar)
items.evidenceFor: better health in adults without symptoms
items.evidenceSummary: Routine health checks in people without symptoms did not lower deaths or heart disease in large trials. A blood test helps most when it finds something you act on.
studiedForms: general health checks with screening tests
items.humanQuestion: Did the last results change anything you do?
items.fitsInstead: A yearly physical with bloodwork, often covered by insurance.
items.notesInternal: Tier C (not D) because blood tests are real diagnostics: they do find low iron, B12 or vitamin D and the result can be acted on. But for population benefit: Krogsbøll 2019 Cochrane (17 trials, ~250,000 people) general health checks had little or no effect on total, cancer or CV mortality (high certainty). USPSTF 2021: insufficient evidence for vitamin D screening in adults without symptoms (I statement). No trials of 100+ marker subscription panels themselves; false positives and follow-up testing are a known downside of broad panels but I did not open a source quantifying it. Morning = fasting draw. Price: functionhealth.com/pricing opened: $365/year (shown as $1/day), 160+ tests, twice a year, so ~$30/month. New overlap group self-tests (with CGM and DNA test) added.

items.name: Continuous glucose monitor (no diabetes)
items.evidenceFor: healthier eating in adults without diabetes
items.evidenceSummary: A 2026 review found few, small studies. Seeing glucose may nudge eating alongside education, but lasting benefit is unproven. Healthy glucose stays in range 96% of the day.
items.humanQuestion: Do the numbers still change what you eat?
items.fitsInstead: A month of wear, then keep the meals you learned from.
items.notesInternal: Tier C: Makkena 2026 Medicina systematic review (12 studies, PROSPERO-registered, no conflicts): two small RCTs showed some dietary changes when CGM was paired with low-GI education (e.g. -15 g carbs over 8 weeks); low certainty for diet, very low for activity and psychosocial outcomes; standalone benefit not established. Shah 2019 JCEM (153 healthy people, blinded Dexcom G6): median 96% of time in 70-140 mg/dL, mean ~98-99 mg/dL, so post-meal rises are normal (supports V3's 'turns normal rises into worry' point, though anxiety itself was not measured there). V3 graded D; I moved to C because two small RCTs exist. Price: stelo.com opened: $89/month subscription (was $99), 15-day sensors, labelled for adults not on insulin. wearable_sees partial: some wearable apps import CGM data. Safety row: Stelo is not for people on insulin or with problematic lows (from Stelo page).

safety.note: Over-the-counter glucose monitors are not made for people on insulin or with frequent lows. A prescription monitor and a diabetes team fit better.

items.name: Consumer DNA wellness test
items.evidenceFor: better diet or weight loss from gene-based advice
items.evidenceSummary: One large trial found gene-matched diet advice did no better than advice based on current eating. Another, in overweight adults, found gene type didn't predict weight loss.
studiedForms: diet advice based on a few diet-related gene variants
items.humanQuestion: Did the report change a single meal?
items.originQuestion: What got you to order the DNA test?
items.fitsInstead: Keep the ancestry part; skip the paid add-on reports.
items.notesInternal: Tier D chosen because the benefit claim rests on mechanism only, while well-run independent RCTs tested it and found no added benefit: Food4Me 2017 (n=1,269 completers, 7 countries) personalised advice beat generic advice, but adding genotype (5 variants) did not improve it further; DIETFITS 2018 JAMA (n=609) no diet x genotype interaction for 12-month weight loss. The tier scale has no 'tested and null' grade; flag for Veer whether this should read N or D. One-off purchase so UNUSED left out. Cost: estimate, ~$100-200 one-off spread over 24 months (V3 typical) ≈ $5; no pricing page opened. Ancestry and raw data are a fair reason to keep; the question focuses on the wellness reports. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Hyperbaric oxygen (wellness use)
items.evidenceFor: recovery, focus or slower ageing in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: Hyperbaric oxygen is real medicine for diving injuries, carbon monoxide and some wounds. The wellness studies, in adults over 64, came from a clinic chain that sells it.
studiedForms: 60 sessions over 3 months in adults over 64 (clinic-run)
items.humanQuestion: Is it the hour of quiet you'd miss?
items.originQuestion: How did you first hear about hyperbaric sessions?
items.notesInternal: Tier N: the only healthy-adult studies I found (Hadanny 2020 RCT n=63 cognition; Hachmo 2020 single-arm n=35 telomeres) are by Efrati's group, authors employed by or shareholders in Aviv Scientific, which sells HBOT longevity programmes, so brand-funded counts as none. Both in adults over 64, not 22-35. Harvard Health 2024 (Catanese, reviewed by Shmerling) lists FDA-cleared uses (decompression sickness, CO poisoning, gas embolism, hard-to-heal wounds, burns, sudden hearing loss etc.), says claims for Alzheimer's, autism, cancer, Lyme are not FDA-approved; risks ear/sinus pain, eardrum rupture, vision change, rarely lung collapse, fire risk; FDA advises accredited facility. FDA's own consumer page returned 404 (moved), so I cite Harvard's summary. Wellness 'mild' soft chambers (~1.3 ATA) were not studied in anything I opened. Cost: estimate, sessions ~$100-250, a few a month; no pricing page opened. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Ear and sinus pressure are common, and pure oxygen is a fire risk. FDA advises an accredited facility for any session.

items.name: Lymphatic drainage massage
items.evidenceFor: less puffiness or better wellbeing in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: The medical version is for lymphedema, and even there it adds only a little to compression. There's no good evidence it de-puffs people without swelling.
studiedForms: manual lymphatic drainage with compression for arm lymphedema
items.humanQuestion: Is it the de-puffing or the quiet hour?
items.originQuestion: Where did lymphatic drainage first come up for you?
items.fitsInstead: A monthly massage you love keeps the quiet hour.
items.notesInternal: Tier D: Ezzo 2015 Cochrane (6 RCTs, breast-cancer lymphedema) MLD added ~7% volume reduction to compression bandaging in 2 small trials; other comparisons not significant or too varied. PubMed search for healthy-subject trials found only small physiology studies (e.g. autonomic/H-reflex changes in J Bodyw Mov Ther 2021, neck MLD in students J Clin Med 2020) with no outcome on puffiness, skin or wellbeing; I read titles/results snippets only, not cited. 'Draining toxins' framing has no support. Area skin because the TikTok draw is de-puffing/face; also mind for the calm. Put in existing massage group (show-together) via overlaps; the group's member list in existing-overlaps.json does not yet include this key, so Veer/Ishan add it there. No safety row: heart failure and active clot are standard contraindications in MLD practice but I did not open a source. Cost: estimate ~$120 a session, about monthly (V3); no pricing page opened. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Colonic or colon cleanse
items.evidenceFor: general health, energy or weight
items.evidenceSummary: No well-run trials support colon cleansing for general health. Case reports describe harms, and early weight loss from cleanses tends to come back. Your liver and kidneys already clear waste.
studiedForms: cleanse diets and laxative products (no controlled trials)
items.humanQuestion: What feeling are you hoping for after?
items.originQuestion: Who first suggested a colon cleanse?
items.fitsInstead: A week of more fibre, water and walks.
items.notesInternal: Tier N: Acosta & Cash 2009 Am J Gastroenterol systematic review found no methodologically rigorous controlled trials for general health, multiple case reports/series of harms. NCCIH 2025: limited evidence for colonic irrigation; serious side effects; harm more likely with GI disease, colon surgery, severe haemorrhoids, kidney disease or heart disease; laxatives cause dehydration; long fasts can upset electrolytes; people with diabetes check with care team; 2017 review: juice/cleanse weight loss mostly regained. Mishori 2011 J Fam Pract (V3 pointer) has no abstract in PubMed and I did not open full text, so not cited. Name avoids the banned word; key kept as given. Cost: estimate ~$100 a session, occasional; no pricing page opened. Safety rows: kidney and heart (clinician-first), diabetes for fasting cleanses, plus a general note.

safety.note: Colon cleansing is more likely to cause harm with kidney disease. Talk with your kidney doctor before any cleanse.
Colon cleansing is more likely to cause harm with heart disease, partly through shifts in fluid and salts. Ask your doctor first.
Fasting and juice cleanses can swing blood sugar. Check with your diabetes care team before starting one.
Colonics and laxative cleanses can cause dehydration and salt imbalance, and case reports describe bowel injury.

items.name: BCAAs (branched-chain amino acid powder)
items.evidenceFor: more muscle or less soreness when daily protein is already enough
items.evidenceSummary: Taken alone, BCAAs don't build muscle; the full set of amino acids in protein does. Pooled trials found less soreness after hard sessions, but the studies vary widely.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the flavored sip mid-session you'd miss?
items.fitsInstead: A protein-rich meal or shake after training covers the same amino acids.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded N and said BCAAs 'add nothing' with enough protein. Muscle side holds: Wolfe 2017 (JISSN review; author discloses industry grants and shares in an amino-acid company) found no human evidence that BCAAs alone raise muscle protein synthesis; the two IV infusion studies saw it fall. ISSN 2017 protein stand (Jager) points to whole protein with all essential amino acids at 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day and does not recommend BCAAs. Plotkin 2021 (IJSNEM narrative review) is relevant but only its abstract without conclusions was reachable, so not cited. Soreness side is not 'nothing': Salem 2024 (Sports Med Open, 18 RCTs, healthy active people, no funding) pooled lower soreness at 24 to 96 h and lower CK at some time points, with high heterogeneity, publication bias, rare allocation concealment, and an internal participant-count mismatch (331 vs 399). Most trials did not equate total protein intake, so soreness may not beat simply eating more protein. Hence C, not N. Overlap: added to the existing protein-powders group (same job: amino acids for training). Price is my estimate for a 30-serving tub (about $25 to $35); no pricing page opened. NOT_TRAINING fits: sold for training only.

items.name: Glutamine (L-glutamine powder)
items.evidenceFor: faster recovery, more muscle or fewer colds in healthy adults who train
items.evidenceSummary: In trials of healthy people who train, glutamine changed neither strength, muscle, body fat nor immune markers. Protein-rich food already supplies plenty of it.
studiedForms: trial doses about 0.1 to 0.9 g per kg a day
items.humanQuestion: What made you start taking it?
items.originQuestion: Who put glutamine on your list?
items.fitsInstead: A protein-rich meal after training already brings glutamine along.
items.notesInternal: V3 N, kept the substance but graded D: trials do exist, and they agree on no benefit, so the only support for the claim is mechanism (plasma glutamine dips after hard exercise). Gleeson 2008 (J Nutr review, abstract): claimed immune, glycogen and anticatabolic benefits have little support in healthy, well-nourished people; 20 to 30 g acutely and 28 g/day for 14 days without ill effect. Ramezani Ahmadi 2019 (Clin Nutr meta-analysis, 25 trials in athletes): no effect on immune system, aerobic performance or body composition; a small weight-reduction signal (-1.36 kg) that the authors note but which is not the reason people buy it. Candow 2001 (RCT, 31 adults 18 to 24, 6 weeks lifting, high dose): no difference in strength, lean mass or protein breakdown. V3's 'gut evidence is from hospital patients only' was not checked here and is left out of the summary. Some small studies report less soreness after eccentric exercise; I found them only via fitness-site summaries, not opened, so not used. Price is my estimate (about $20 for a month of 5 g); no pricing page opened. Moment set to evening (post-workout or bedtime use is common), a judgment call.

items.name: ZMA (zinc, magnesium and vitamin B6)
items.evidenceFor: higher testosterone, strength or better sleep in people already getting enough zinc and magnesium
items.evidenceSummary: Trials in men eating enough zinc found no rise in testosterone or strength, and two nights of ZMA left sleep unchanged. The magnesium inside is the part with sleep research.
items.humanQuestion: Do you take it for sleep or training?
items.originQuestion: Where did you first hear about ZMA?
items.fitsInstead: Plain magnesium at bedtime keeps the ritual with fewer ingredients.
items.notesInternal: V3 N; graded D. The testosterone claim traces to Brilla & Conte 2000 (not opened here; reported by Wilborn as finding higher free testosterone, IGF-1 and strength in football players). Replications: Wilborn 2004 (JISSN RCT, 42 trained men, 8 weeks, funded by Cytodyne, which made the product tested; null for hormones, body composition and strength) and Koehler 2009 (EJCN, 14 exercising men with adequate zinc intake; no change in total or free testosterone). Edwards 2024 (Nutrients, 19 recreationally trained men with adequate intake, two nights, actigraphy) found no sleep effect. I chose D over C because the independent trials agree on no benefit; the claim rests on one unreplicated trial plus mechanism. Dose from Wilborn's product (30 mg zinc, 450 mg magnesium, 11 mg B6), a standard ZMA label. Overlap: already in the magnesium keep-one group. Safety: 30 mg zinc plus a zinc-containing multivitamin pushes intake high; I could not open the NIH ODS zinc sheet (Cloudflare block) to cite the 40 mg adult UL, so the safety note avoids the number and leans on a 2025 case report of zinc-induced copper deficiency. Price is my estimate (about $15 to $20 a month); no pricing page opened. Wearable partial: sleep tracking would show any change.

safety.note: ZMA holds about 30 mg of zinc. Years of high zinc can lower copper, and a multivitamin adds more zinc on top.

items.name: Testosterone supplement (tribulus, fenugreek, D-aspartic acid blends)
items.evidenceFor: higher testosterone or bigger training gains in healthy men
items.evidenceSummary: Tribulus and D-aspartic acid didn't raise testosterone in trials. Four fenugreek trials, pooled, showed a rise. Most blends hold untested ingredients, some above safe vitamin and mineral limits.
items.humanQuestion: What were you hoping to feel from it?
items.notesInternal: V3 graded N and said fenugreek has 'none on testosterone'; that part is contradicted: Mansoori 2020 (Phytother Res meta-analysis, 4 RCTs) found a significant rise in total testosterone. I only read the abstract, which gives no effect size or funding; fenugreek trials are commonly run with branded extracts, so check before upgrading. Tribulus: Qureshi 2014 systematic review (11 studies) found it ineffective in humans except within combined supplements. D-AA: Willoughby & Leutholtz 2013 (3 g, 28 days, trained men) and Melville 2017 (6 g, 12 weeks, 22 trained men aged 18 to 36) both found no change in testosterone or training outcomes. Clemesha 2020 (50 products): 61.5% of 109 components had no testosterone data, 10.1% had data showing a decrease, and 13 products exceeded the UL for zinc, B3 or magnesium. Tier C because the ingredients disagree (fenugreek positive, tribulus and D-AA null) and no blend has been tested. No dose fields: blends vary too much. fits_instead left empty: I found no source for a lifestyle swap that raises testosterone in healthy young men. Price: V3's $40, my estimate; no pricing page opened. Area move because the purchase is about training and physique. Name and short_name avoid 'booster' because 'boost' is on the banned word list. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Fenugreek above food amounts is not considered safe in pregnancy.
Large doses of fenugreek can drop blood sugar, so with diabetes medicine a clinician check comes first.
Some blends carry zinc, B3 or magnesium above daily upper limits, so the label is worth a look.

items.name: Fat burner or thermogenic pills
items.evidenceFor: meaningful fat loss beyond diet and exercise
items.evidenceSummary: Caffeine and green tea nudge fat burning slightly, yet trials show little weight change. Weight-loss and energy pills cause most supplement-related ER visits for a racing heart.
studiedForms: multi-ingredient thermogenic blends (rarely tested as products)
items.humanQuestion: Do you feel it more in energy or appetite?
items.fitsInstead: A morning coffee gives the same caffeine lift.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded N; I graded C because caffeine and green tea do have trial data, just small effects. Jeukendrup & Randell 2011 (Obes Rev review): only caffeine and green tea have data backing fat-metabolism effects; evidence lacking for carnitine, CLA, forskolin, chromium and others. Tabrizi 2019 (13 RCTs, 606 people, I2 above 90%): caffeine might promote weight, BMI and fat reduction; very heterogeneous. Jurgens 2012 Cochrane: green tea outside Japan, -0.04 kg over 12 weeks, not meaningful. Batsis 2021 (Obesity, 315 RCTs of supplements and alternative therapies): only 52 low-risk and sufficient, of which 16 showed weight differences of 0.3 to 4.93 kg. Geller 2015 (NEJM, ED surveillance 2004 to 2013, HHS-funded): weight-loss or energy products caused 71.8% of supplement adverse events with palpitations, chest pain or tachycardia, 58% in people aged 20 to 34. V3 said they 'disturb your sleep': true by way of caffeine, but I did not open a fat-burner sleep study, so the summary leaves it out; added to the evening-stimulants overlap group instead. Coffee swap is my inference from shared caffeine. Under-18 safety row not added because I did not open a pediatric source this round (AAP 2011 exists in the table for energy drinks; Ishan may want it extended). Price: V3's $40, my estimate. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Weight-loss and energy pills cause most supplement-related ER visits for a racing heart or chest pain, so a clinician check comes first.
FDA suggests asking a provider about caffeine in pregnancy, and these pills often carry a lot of it.
FDA suggests talking with a provider about caffeine limits while breastfeeding.
Some medicines make caffeine stronger, so a pharmacist can say whether these pills fit.

items.name: Nootropic stack (alpha-GPC and similar focus blends)
items.evidenceFor: sharper focus or memory in healthy young adults
