items.evidenceSummary: In healthy young adults, most supplement trials for thinking are small and low quality. Caffeine, alone or with L-theanine, has the clearest short-term lift. Whole stacks lack independent trials.
items.humanQuestion: Which days do you reach for it most?
items.fitsInstead: A morning coffee covers the best-studied part, the caffeine.
items.notesInternal: V3 C, kept. Pomeroy 2020 (Nutrients systematic review, 37 studies, healthy adults 18 to 35): 73% low quality; only tyrosine or caffeine supported, mainly under sleep loss. Camfield 2014 (Nutr Rev meta-analysis, 11 RCTs): caffeine plus L-theanine gave moderate gains in alertness and attention switching within 2 h, driven more by caffeine dose. Alpha-GPC: Marcus 2017 (JISSN, 48 college men, 7 days) found no change in psychomotor vigilance and a jump-power gain at 250 mg, not 500 mg; it lowered TSH at 500 mg. Lee 2021 (JAMA Netw Open, 12 million Koreans over 50, prescribed alpha-GPC): 43% higher 10-year stroke risk, dose-response; observational and older population, so used only for the heart safety row, not the tier. Cohen 2021 (Neurol Clin Pract): 10 cognitive supplements contained 5 unapproved drugs, some undeclared, 75% of quantities inaccurate. Stacks vary widely (some have caffeine; those would also belong in evening-stimulants, not added here since many don't). Price: V3's $60, my estimate; the Onnit page I opened showed no price.

safety.note: In a large study of adults over 50, alpha-GPC users had more strokes, so a clinician check comes first.
Lab tests found unlisted, unapproved drugs in some focus supplements, at drug-level doses.

items.name: Electrolyte mix plus a sports drink
items.evidenceFor: holding fluid and keeping pace in sessions over about an hour or with heavy sweating
items.evidenceSummary: For long or very sweaty sessions, sodium and carbs help, a use sports medicine groups support. Both drinks carry the same salts, so one usually covers it.
items.humanQuestion: Do you use both on long, sweaty days?
items.fitsInstead: One drink for long, sweaty sessions; water the rest of the time.
items.notesInternal: NUANCE: the B holds only for sessions over about an hour or heavy sweating, not any training. The allowed evidence_requires values cannot say 'long or sweaty', so I used 'trains' as the closest and set tier_otherwise C. The engine should read TRAINS here narrowly: a 40-minute lift does not earn the keep, and for short sessions the C (and water) applies. Until the schema can express duration, the OVERLAP lever (electrolytes group, keep-one with electrolytes-lmnt-etc) is the main point of this row: two products doing one job. Sources: Sawka 2007 ACSM stand (abstract only; the numeric sodium advice is paywalled): electrolyte and carbohydrate drinks can beat water 'under certain circumstances', with customised plans because sweat rates vary. Stellingwerff & Cox 2014 (61 RCTs, 679 people): 82% showed carbohydrate improved performance, with gains growing with exercise duration; under about an hour the effect is a mouth-sensing one. Kind is food-drink, so no dose_min; the sibling row electrolytes-lmnt-etc carries the sodium dose (500 to 700 mg/L, ACSM 1996). Safety rows mirror the sibling row's sourced ones (He 2013, NKF), which I did not reopen. Sugar in sports drinks (diabetes) not graded. Price is my estimate: about $45 for a month of an electrolyte mix plus about $15 of sports drinks; no pricing page opened. V3's 'two sources of the same salts and sugar' is fair (mixes like LMNT are sugar-free, so 'sugar' applies only to the sports drink).

safety.note: Two drinks double the sodium, and more sodium tends to mean higher blood pressure, so a clinician check comes first.
Kidneys that filter less can let sodium, fluid and potassium build up, so the kidney care team gets the first say.

items.name: Mushroom coffee (Ryze, Four Sigmatic and similar)
items.evidenceFor: sharper focus or calmer energy from the mushrooms at the amounts in a cup
items.evidenceSummary: One small trial found 1.8 g of lion's mane sped one attention task. A popular blend splits about 2 g across six mushrooms, with about half a coffee's caffeine.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the mushrooms, or the gentler cup?
items.originQuestion: Where did mushroom coffee first catch your eye?
items.fitsInstead: Half-caf coffee keeps the gentler morning cup.
items.notesInternal: V3 D, kept. No trial of any mushroom coffee product found. Ingredient evidence: Docherty 2023 (Nutrients pilot RCT, 41 healthy adults 18 to 45, 1.8 g lion's mane): faster Stroop at 60 min after one dose, a non-significant trend to less stress at 28 days, plus null and some negative findings. Mori 2009 (older adults with MCI, 3 g/day) is not the target group, so not cited. Menon 2025 systematic review: 5 RCTs, mostly cognition in people with and without dementia; side effects include stomach upset, headache, allergy. Ryze holds about 2 g of a six-mushroom blend and 48 mg caffeine per serving (company figures via a nutritionist's review updated March 2024; per-mushroom amounts undisclosed; the 0.33 g each figure would be an equal-split assumption, so the summary avoids it). D rather than C because no study tested these amounts; the lion's mane pilot used close to a whole cup's blend of one mushroom. Price: Ryze product page, $45 list for 30 servings ($27 on a sale when opened). Caffeine is roughly half a cup, so this row's real sleep effect is gentler than coffee; it stays in evening-stimulants. A 2026 case report of shiitake dermatitis from mushroom coffee exists (abstract unavailable), so no safety row.

items.name: Sea moss (gel or capsules)
items.evidenceFor: general health, skin and mineral intake
items.evidenceSummary: No human trials of sea moss itself. Seaweed products' iodine swings widely, and lab tests found arsenic, mercury and bacteria in some sea moss.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the minerals you want, or the morning routine?
items.originQuestion: Who got you onto sea moss?
items.fitsInstead: Iodised salt and a varied diet cover iodine more steadily.
items.notesInternal: Tier D: searched Europe PMC for human trials of Chondrus crispus / sea moss / Irish moss and found none (only cow and hen feeding studies). Claims rest on mineral content, i.e. mechanism and anecdote. Safety evidence is real: Aakre 2021 (Norwegian market, not sea moss specifically, mostly kelps) shows seaweed iodine per serving often exceeds the UL; Rejuso 2026 is the first US sea moss product survey (66 products) with arsenic/cobalt/mercury in dried product and Salmonella/Cronobacter isolates. I could NOT open the NIH ODS iodine fact sheet (Cloudflare 403), so the adult UL (1,100 mcg) is not cited here; worth adding nih-ods iodine if another agent has it. Did not find a sea moss-specific iodine assay paper. Could arguably join daily-multivitamin overlap ('92 minerals' marketing) but I left overlaps empty since that group's members list doesn't include it. Price is an estimate (gels often $25 to $40 a jar), no pricing page opened. Rewrote fits_instead to avoid a claim I can't source about health benefit. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Sea moss iodine varies widely and can upset thyroid levels. Check first if you take thyroid medicine.
Iodine matters in pregnancy, but sea moss amounts are unpredictable and can run far above the safe upper limit. Ask first.
Lab tests found arsenic, mercury and bacteria in some store-bought sea moss. Quality varies a lot between brands.

items.name: Shilajit (resin or capsules)
items.evidenceFor: testosterone and energy in healthy men
items.evidenceSummary: Every human trial found was run or paid for by a shilajit brand. Lab tests have found thallium, a toxic metal, in raw resin and capsules.
items.humanQuestion: Has your jar been tested for heavy metals?
items.originQuestion: What first put shilajit on your radar?
items.notesInternal: Tier N. Pandit 2016 (Andrologia, PrimaVie) lists Natreon Inc as funder in Europe PMC grant data, so it counts as none. Yadav 2026 (TruBlk resin) is open-label, single-arm, and 4 of 6 authors are at Amaara Botanicals (the brand). A 2026 TruBlk RCT is a preprint by the same group (not opened). Martinez 2025 RCT tested chromium + amla + shilajit together (not opened, combination, can't isolate). Morgado 2024 rates PrimaVie 'possibly effective' in low-T men, but that rests on brand trials. V3 claimed raw shilajit 'repeatedly' contains lead and arsenic: I could not verify that for shilajit specifically; I did find Kamgar 2025 (thallium in raw and supplement shilajit). Safety row is a note to buy tested product. Price estimate (resin jars roughly $30 to $60 for a month); vendor page I opened showed no price.

safety.note: Choose a product tested for heavy metals. Lab tests have found thallium in raw shilajit and in supplements.

items.name: Lion's mane mushroom (capsules or powder)
items.evidenceFor: focus and memory in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: Small trials in healthy adults found little: one faster attention task, no overall memory or mood gain. Slightly better signals in older adults with memory decline.
studiedForms: fruiting body or mycelium extract capsules
items.humanQuestion: Have you noticed sharper focus since starting?
items.fitsInstead: Cooked lion's mane mushrooms keep it as food.
items.notesInternal: Tier C, kept from V3 but for a reason V3 didn't give: in healthy young adults there are now two small RCTs. Docherty 2023 (n=41, 1.8 g/day, product donated by Sempera Organics, no other funding, read full text) found one acute Stroop speed effect, recall slightly worse, no 28-day effect, stress only a trend (p=0.051). Surendran 2025 (n=18 crossover, 3 g extract) found no overall effect; I checked full text: two authors are employed by Three Spirit Drinks (lion's mane drinks), which paid publication fees, so I marked it brand_funded yes. Menon 2025 SR: MMSE +1.17 pooled from one RCT + one pilot in older/dementia groups. Also saw (not cited) Evans 2026 n=10 uncontrolled pilot, no significant change, and a 2026 preprint RCT. Could be argued down to D for healthy adults; I kept C because independent RCTs exist and disagree slightly. Price estimate.

items.name: Maca root powder or capsules
items.evidenceFor: sex drive in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: A few small trials suggest a modest lift in sex drive. Reviews call the evidence too thin to be sure, and maca isn't shown to raise testosterone.
studiedForms: gelatinised or raw maca root powder
items.humanQuestion: Is it for sex drive, or for energy?
items.notesInternal: Tier C. Shin 2010 SR (full text): 4 RCTs, 131 people, none reported allocation concealment; 3 of 4 showed a benefit on desire/function, cyclists none. Ho 2026 meta of herbal ED supplements (14 RCTs) says maca evidence remains insufficient. Morgado 2024 included 2 Lepidium meyenii testosterone studies and did not list maca among effective boosters (abstract only; I did not see maca-specific numbers, so the summary says 'isn't shown to raise' rather than 'doesn't'). Also saw a 2024 maca physical-performance meta (Huerta Ojeda, animals and humans) but did not open. Price estimate. Put in testosterone-boosters overlap because it's marketed on libido alongside tongkat and shilajit; Veer may prefer to leave it out.

items.name: Bovine colostrum powder
items.evidenceFor: fewer days with cold symptoms in adults who train regularly
items.evidenceSummary: In people who train, small trials of 10 to 20 g daily found fewer days with cold symptoms. Gut, skin and general wellness claims are largely untested.
items.humanQuestion: How many hours a week do you train?
items.notesInternal: Tier C for trainers, D otherwise. Jones 2016 meta (full text): 5 RCTs, 152 endurance-training adults, URS days rate ratio 0.56, URS episodes 0.62; 4 of 5 trials moderate/high risk of bias. Competing interests: lead author's PhD was partly supported via a project with The Golden Dairy Ltd (colostrum supplier for Neovite); trials used donated product. I marked the meta brand_funded no, but Veer may want to treat it as brand-linked, which would push this toward N. V3 said it helps athletes' gut problems: Aitkenhead 2025 meta of supplements for exercise gut damage found no pooled benefit and clinically trivial changes (abstract doesn't break out colostrum, so I don't claim colostrum failed specifically). Goluch 2026: body fat and lipid results inconsistent. tier_otherwise D because the feed claims (gut lining, skin, immunity in non-athletes) rest on mechanism. dose_min 10 g from the lowest trial dose; popular feed brands appear to serve much less per scoop (I could not open ARMRA's page, 404), so DOSE_BELOW_MIN may often fire; verify a serving size before relying on it. Price is an estimate based on premium feed brands (~$2 to $3 a serving).

safety.note: Colostrum is cow's milk. Skip it with a milk allergy.

items.name: NMN or NR (NAD precursors)
items.evidenceFor: energy, metabolic health and healthy ageing in adults
items.evidenceSummary: It reliably raises NAD in the blood. Trials of energy, blood sugar and weight mostly found no change, with a possible endurance signal. Longer-life findings come from mice.
items.humanQuestion: What made you start: energy, or ageing?
items.notesInternal: Moved from V3 D to C: there are now ~28 randomized human trials, so 'mechanism/animal only' no longer fits; they mostly show target engagement with null or inconsistent outcomes. Yang 2026 NMN meta (15 RCTs): no effect on weight, BMI, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, SBP; DBP slightly lower. Gallagher 2026 SR: 33 human studies, functional outcomes 'heterogeneous and often null'. Gao 2026 NMA: no precursor helps perceived fatigue or sleep; NMN linked to endurance (could be small-study effect). I didn't separately open Yoshino 2021 (V3 hint). Many NR trials are ChromaDex-supported; I didn't audit funding trial by trial, which could argue for a lower tier. 'Longer-life findings come from mice' rests on Gallagher's rodent findings; Gallagher's abstract says rodent improvements, not lifespan explicitly; Veer may soften to 'animal studies'. Price: Tru Niagen 300 mg/day lists $49 (from $39.20 subscribed) on truniagen.com, opened 2026-10-22; NMN products vary, so $45 is a midpoint.

items.name: Berberine
items.evidenceFor: blood sugar and weight in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: Good trials show lower blood sugar in people with raised levels or type 2 diabetes. For healthy adults, there is little evidence of benefit.
items.doseTypical: 500 mg two or three times daily with meals
items.humanQuestion: Is it for blood sugar, or for weight?
items.notesInternal: Tier B, but read this: the evidence is in people with raised glucose, T2D, metabolic syndrome or PCOS (Zhao 2023: 20 RCTs n=1,761, FPG -0.52 mmol/L, larger in diabetes; Liu 2025: 12 RCTs n=889, 300 to 1,500 mg/day; Elahi Vahed 2026: 23 RCTs, weight -0.88 kg). For a healthy 25-year-old taking it as 'nature's Ozempic' the tier would be C at best. evidence_requires has no code for 'has a condition' (only none/trains/deficiency/low_intake), so I left it none and tier B, which means it is protected for everyone. Suggest Ishan adds a code like raised_glucose with tier_otherwise C. Interactions are real: Dumitru 2026 review (CYP3A4/2D6/2C9, P-gp, OCT/MATE, additive hypoglycaemia; cyclosporine +34.5% AUC in transplant patients). NCCIH goldenseal page: metformin levels fell ~25% in healthy adults; no pregnancy/breastfeeding. Mostly Chinese trials, quality uneven. dose_min 300 is the lowest dose in Liu's included trials; most trials used 900 to 1,500 mg/day. Price: Thorne Berberine-500, $44 for 30 servings (thorne.com, opened 2026-10-22).

safety.note: Berberine lowers blood sugar and can add to diabetes medicine, raising the chance of lows. It can also change metformin levels. Ask your prescriber first.
Berberine changes how the body handles many medicines, including cyclosporine. Check with a pharmacist or clinician before combining.
Berberine can harm newborns. Not for use in pregnancy.
Berberine can harm newborns. Not for use while breastfeeding.

items.name: Resveratrol
items.evidenceFor: heart and metabolic health in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: Trials show small shifts in waist, cholesterol and blood pressure, mostly in people with diabetes or extra weight. Longer-life findings come from simpler organisms, not people.
items.humanQuestion: What were you hoping it would do?
items.fitsInstead: Grapes and berries carry resveratrol as everyday food.
items.notesInternal: Moved from V3 N to C: there are many independent RCTs, so N (no independent studies) was wrong. Sun 2026 umbrella (45 meta-analyses): only four high-certainty effects, all small and in narrower groups (waist -0.8 cm; TC in overweight; BP in T2D). Cochrane 2020 (T2D): 3 tiny RCTs, insufficient. Semba 2014 InCHIANTI cohort: dietary resveratrol not associated with mortality, CVD, cancer or inflammation; this is diet-level, not supplement dose. V3 cited a Cochrane review on CVD primary prevention and Berman 2017; I did not find/open either. The 'simpler organisms' line comes from Semba's background statement; no lifespan source opened beyond that. Dose range from Cochrane trials (10 to 1,000 mg) and typical labels; label range not sourced. Price estimate.

items.name: Tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia)
items.evidenceFor: testosterone in healthy men
items.evidenceSummary: Small trials report higher testosterone, clearest in men with low levels. Most used one company's extract, and trials in healthy men were mixed.
items.humanQuestion: Have you had your testosterone checked?
items.notesInternal: Tier C, borderline N. Leisegang 2022 meta (full text, no funding, no COI): 5 RCTs n=232, SMD 1.35; 7 of 9 included studies used Physta (Biotropics Malaysia), and Biotropics staff (A. George) co-author several (Chinnappan 2021, Ismail 2012, George 2013). If brand-authored Physta trials count as none, what's left in healthy men is small: Quin 2021 (n=21, not significant) and Chan 2021 (Physta, authorship unclear). In healthy men with normal T, Ismail 2012 and George 2013 found no significant change; Chinnappan 2021 (men 50 to 70 with low baseline T ~190 ng/dL) found a rise. Leitao 2021 (independent, men with androgen deficiency) positive. So 'mixed in healthy men' is accurate. Morgado 2024 rates it possibly effective for healthy and low-T men. No safety row: I did not open a liver or interaction source for tongkat. Price estimate.

items.name: DHEA or pregnenolone
items.evidenceFor: energy, libido and body composition in adults
items.evidenceSummary: DHEA is a hormone precursor that raises testosterone and estrogen. Trials, mostly in older adults, found no clear gain in libido, fitness, body composition or quality of life.
items.humanQuestion: Did a clinician suggest it after bloodwork?
items.notesInternal: Tier C, bordering D for this audience: RCTs exist but are in older adults and mostly null (Nair 2006 NEJM 2-year RCT; Elraiyah 2014 meta, libido p=0.06, low certainty). No trials found in 22 to 35 year olds. He 2025 meta confirms it is hormonally active (raises T and E2, more at >=50 mg). Pregnenolone: search found RCTs only in alcohol and cocaine use disorder (Milivojevic/Sinha lab, titles seen, not opened), nothing in healthy adults, so no pregnenolone tier claim made. NCCIH DHEA page returned 404; MedlinePlus monograph withdrawn (TRC database unavailable since July 2025), so safety rows lean on Harvard Health (Jan 2025, physician-reviewed). If a clinician prescribed it (adrenal insufficiency, IVF), that's clinician-led care, not this row; the engine may want a never_clear path for that. Not marking never_clear here since the feed version is self-started. Price estimate (DHEA is cheap, ~$10 to $20).

safety.note: DHEA is a hormone precursor. Not for use in pregnancy.
DHEA is a hormone precursor. Not for use while breastfeeding.
DHEA is advised against with liver problems.
DHEA can interact with blood thinners, hormone therapy, some cancer medicines and antidepressants. Ask a clinician first.
DHEA can shift mood. Talk to a clinician first if you live with a mood condition.
DHEA raises testosterone and estrogen. Acne and mood changes are common side effects. Skip it with PCOS or a hormone-sensitive cancer.

items.name: Green tea extract (EGCG capsules)
items.evidenceFor: weight loss in adults with overweight
items.evidenceSummary: Outside Japan, trials found almost no weight change. Extracts have been linked to liver injury, and fasting raises how much gets absorbed.
items.humanQuestion: Do you take it with food?
items.fitsInstead: Brewed green tea keeps the habit, with a long safety record.
items.notesInternal: Tier C on weight: Cochrane 2012 (Jurgens) found -0.04 kg outside Japan (6 RCTs, n=532), Japanese trials -0.2 to -3.5 kg but unpoolable; authors judge it not clinically important. Could be argued D-for-effect but trials exist and disagree by region, so C. Liver: EFSA 2018 says >=800 mg EGCG/day as supplement raised transaminases in trials; USP 2020 review: liver injury case reports at 140 to ~1,000 mg EGCG/day, fasting bolus dosing raises EGCG bioavailability; USP label requires 'take with food, do not use with liver problems'. Brewed tea is generally safe per EFSA (rare idiosyncratic cases). V3 referenced Hu 2018 hepatotoxicity review; I used the USP 2020 review (Oketch-Rabah) instead, which I opened. Price estimate. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Concentrated green tea extract has been linked to liver injury. Skip it with any liver condition.
Take it with food, not on an empty stomach. Stop and see a clinician if dark urine, belly pain or yellow skin appear.

items.name: L-theanine
items.evidenceFor: self-rated sleep quality in adults
items.evidenceSummary: A 2025 review of 19 trials found small gains in self-rated sleep and next-day feel. Few tested L-theanine alone.
studiedForms: many trials used blends with other ingredients
items.humanQuestion: Do you take it for sleep, or with coffee?
items.notesInternal: Tier C. Bulman/D'Cunha 2025 Sleep Med Rev meta-analysis (abstract via Bond portal): 19 RCTs, n=897, 18 pooled. Significant but small subjective effects: sleep onset latency SMD 0.15 (CI 0.01-0.29), daytime dysfunction 0.33, overall sleep quality 0.43 (CI 0.04-0.83). Authors flag few pure L-theanine studies and unsettled dose. No objective outcomes in abstract. Borderline B for self-rated sleep; kept C because effects are small, subjective, and confounded by blends. Dose 200-400 mg from V3 and Cotter 2025 review (search snippet only, not opened). Moment 'morning' added because many take it with coffee; caffeine-pairing evidence not reviewed here. Price is an estimate (~$12-18/month for 200 mg daily at mainstream brands); no pricing page opened. No safety row: nothing serious found in opened sources. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Glycine
items.evidenceFor: falling asleep sooner and next-day alertness
items.evidenceSummary: Small Japanese trials found 3 g at bedtime helped people fall asleep sooner and feel less tired. Each involved researchers from a glycine maker; no independent trial yet.
items.humanQuestion: Do you fall asleep sooner on glycine nights?
items.originQuestion: Where did glycine at bedtime come from?
items.notesInternal: Tier N by the brief's rule (brand-affiliated only counts as none), but this is a judgement call: V3 had C. The human sleep trials (Inagawa 2006, Yamadera 2007, Bannai 2012) all include Ajinomoto researchers; Ajinomoto sells glycine. Bannai 2012 full text: single-blind crossover, 7 analysed, all Ajinomoto employees, 3 g 30 min before bed after sleep restriction; day-1 fatigue and PVT improved, most other measures not. Yamadera 2007 (Sleep Biol Rhythms 5:126-131, co-authors Inagawa and Bannai of Ajinomoto): only Crossref metadata opened, no abstract, so not cited as a source. Soh 2024 GeroScience systematic review (abstract, independent): sleep gains in healthy adults came from small, high-risk-of-bias studies. If Veer prefers to count academic first authors as independent, regrade to C and drop BORROWED_WEAK rationale accordingly (BORROWED_WEAK still allowed at C). Price estimate (~$10/month for 3 g/day powder); no page opened.

items.name: Tart cherry juice or extract
items.evidenceFor: longer, better sleep in adults
items.evidenceSummary: Tiny trials of 8 to 20 people found longer sleep. Larger, later trials of juice and capsules found no change. A 2025 review called the evidence limited.
items.doseTypical: 240 ml juice twice daily, or 500 mg capsule
studiedForms: Montmorency tart cherry juice or concentrate
items.humanQuestion: Is it the juice you like, or the sleep?
items.fitsInstead: One small glass, rather than two, keeps the ritual with less sugar.
items.notesInternal: Tier C: studies disagree. Positives: Howatson 2012 (n=20 healthy, 7 days concentrate, more total sleep and efficiency, urinary melatonin up; funding not stated in record), Losso 2018 (8 completers >50 with insomnia, 240 ml twice daily, ~84 min more PSG sleep; NIH-funded), Pigeon 2010 (n=15 older insomnia, only WASO improved; seen in listing, not cited). Nulls: Hillman 2022 (n=44 healthy, 30 days juice or capsules) and Tucker 2024 (n=34, 500 mg capsules) found no sleep effect, both funded by Cherry Marketing Institute (industry funding of null results). Barforoush 2025 review of 7 studies: limited and heterogeneous. A 2023 meta-analysis (Springer, objective efficiency ES 0.63) was seen in search only, not opened. also_serves 'move' because it's also used for exercise recovery (not reviewed here). Overlap: tart cherry is NOT yet a member of sleep-aids in existing-overlaps.json; Ishan needs to add it or drop OVERLAP. Sugar note: V3's ~25 g sugar per serving not verified on a label. Price estimate (~$25-45/month for concentrate twice daily, less for capsules).

safety.note: Tart cherry juice carries natural sugar, and two glasses a day add up. Capsules skip the sugar.

items.name: CBD (gummies or oil)
items.evidenceFor: better sleep in adults with insomnia
items.evidenceSummary: Sleep trials used high doses, far above most gummies, and still mostly matched placebo. In one test of online products, only 31% matched the label.
items.doseTypical: 10 to 50 in gummies; 150 to 300 in trials
studiedForms: one trial used CBD with terpenes
items.humanQuestion: How many milligrams is each gummy, roughly?
items.fitsInstead: Chamomile tea keeps the night ritual for far less.
items.notesInternal: Tier C. Suraev 2020 Sleep Med Rev systematic review: insufficient evidence for any sleep disorder, moderate-high risk of bias. Narayan 2024 JCSM RCT (n=30 insomnia, 150 mg nightly x2 weeks): no difference on ISI, self-reported SOL, SE, WASO; objective SE higher at 2 weeks; well-being higher. Wang 2025 JCSM (n=125, 300 mg CBD+terpenes, crossover) found a small rise in % deep+REM on a wrist tracker, no change in total sleep; funding not visible in the record, so not cited. Suraev CANSLEEP (200 mg CBD + 10 mg THC) cut total sleep and REM (conference abstract, not cited). dose_min 150 = lowest pure-CBD dose in an opened sleep RCT, used so DOSE_BELOW_MIN can flag 10-25 mg gummies; it is not a recommendation to take more. Bonn-Miller 2017 JAMA: 84 online products, 31% accurate within 10%, 43% under-labelled, 26% over-labelled, 21% had THC. Safety from NCCIH (interactions, liver injury) and FDA 2019 (avoid in pregnancy/breastfeeding). Price estimate (~$40-60/month for a 25 mg daily gummy). Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: CBD can change how other medicines act in the body. A pharmacist can check your list first.
CBD has been linked to liver test changes and liver injury. With a liver condition, a clinician is the first stop.
The FDA advises against CBD in any form during pregnancy.
The FDA advises against CBD while breastfeeding; some passes into breast milk.
About one in five CBD products tested held THC, not always on the label. Worth knowing before a drug test.

items.name: Kava (drink or capsules)
items.evidenceFor: short-term relief of anxiety
items.evidenceSummary: Early trials in anxious patients found short-term relief, but a 16-week trial of 171 adults with diagnosed anxiety found no benefit over placebo. Rare liver injury is reported.
studiedForms: water-extracted root extract tablets standardised to kavalactones
items.humanQuestion: Is kava for winding down, or for company?
items.fitsInstead: Chamomile tea keeps the evening wind-down, without the liver questions.
items.notesInternal: V3 had B; downgraded to C because studies now disagree. Pittler & Ernst 2003 Cochrane (Europe PMC record; Cochrane site returned 403): 11 RCTs, n=645, HAM-A WMD 5.0 (CI 1.1-8.8) for kava, short-term use relatively safe; the review is old and Cochrane marks its CAM summaries outdated. Sarris 2013 (n=58 analysed, 120-240 mg, d=0.62) was positive, but the larger phase III Sarris 2020 (n=171 GAD, 240 mg/day, 16 weeks) found no benefit (placebo slightly better), with more liver-test abnormalities on kava. NCCIH 2025: may help anxiety, not GAD; rare serious liver injury; avoid with alcohol or sedatives; pregnancy/breastfeeding risks. Teschke 2008: of 26 suspected liver cases, 8 possible/probable, mostly with overdose, long use or co-medication. Sleep: found no solid kava sleep trials. Area set to mind (anxiety is the evidence outcome), also_serves sleep. Cadence 'occasional' and why_loved 'connection' reflect kava-bar culture; capsule users may be daily. Price estimate (~$25-35/month capsules; kava bar shells cost more). Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Kava has been linked to rare, sometimes serious liver injury. With any liver condition, a clinician is the first stop.
Kava adds to sedatives and can interact with other medicines. Worth a check with a pharmacist or clinician first.
Kava with alcohol is linked to more liver problems and heavier sedation. Kava nights go best alcohol-free.
Kava may carry special risks in pregnancy. A clinician is the first stop.
Kava may carry special risks while breastfeeding. A clinician is the first stop.

items.name: Apigenin
items.evidenceFor: falling or staying asleep in adults
items.evidenceSummary: No human trial has tested apigenin alone for sleep. In mice it acts on calming brain receptors. Chamomile, its main food source, has small trials of its own.
studiedForms: in humans only inside multi-ingredient blends
items.humanQuestion: Did this come from a podcast sleep stack?
items.originQuestion: Did apigenin come from a podcast sleep stack, or somewhere else?
items.fitsInstead: Chamomile tea is the everyday source of apigenin.
items.notesInternal: Tier D. Europe PMC search (apigenin + sleep + human) found no RCT of apigenin alone. Viola 1995: apigenin isolated from chamomile binds the benzodiazepine receptor, anxiolytic in mice, sedative only at 10x dose. Mastrofini 2026 JISSN RCT (n=103 active adults): evening blend had 50 mg apigenin plus magnesium L-threonate and L-theanine, so apigenin's own effect can't be separated; funding not visible in the record. Wong 2026 mouse study: apigenin + magnesium synergy (animal). Popularity traces to a podcast sleep protocol (not sourced, from V3). Price estimate (~$15-25/month for 50 mg). No safety row: no specific harm found in opened sources. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: GABA (oral supplement)
items.evidenceFor: falling asleep sooner or sleeping better
items.evidenceSummary: A 2020 review of 14 trials found very limited evidence for sleep. Whether swallowed GABA reaches the brain is still unsettled, and many studies had seller ties.
items.humanQuestion: Do you feel a difference on nights without it?
items.fitsInstead: Chamomile tea keeps the bedtime ritual.
items.notesInternal: Tier C (V3 had D): human placebo-controlled trials exist but are small and disagree. Hepsomali 2020 Front Neurosci systematic review: 14 placebo-controlled trials, 'limited' evidence for stress and 'very limited' for sleep (first author's affiliation Unilever, not a GABA seller). Boonstra 2015 Front Psychol: blood-brain barrier crossing long assumed impossible, studies contradictory; much calming evidence from researchers with potential conflicts. FORM_NOT_ABSORBED not used because the barrier question is unresolved, not disproven. Could be argued N if every sleep trial is seller-funded; I did not verify funding trial by trial. Dose range from V3 plus common product labels (not opened). Overlap: gaba-oral is NOT yet in sleep-aids in existing-overlaps.json; needs adding or drop OVERLAP. Price estimate. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: 5-HTP
items.evidenceFor: falling or staying asleep in adults
items.evidenceSummary: There are no good trials of 5-HTP for adult sleep. Evidence for mood rests on a few small, weak trials. It can clash with antidepressants.
items.humanQuestion: Is it for sleep, or for mood?
items.originQuestion: Who suggested 5-HTP to you?
items.fitsInstead: A short worry list before bed keeps the wind-down, no capsule.

swap.title: A short worry list before bed

items.notesInternal: Tier D for adult sleep. MSK About Herbs (updated 2022, full page): 'studies evaluating 5-HTP for insomnia are lacking'; avoid with SSRIs, MAOIs, tricyclics without physician; case reports of serotonin syndrome (with linezolid), mania (with MAOI), scleroderma-like illness (with carbidopa), and eosinophilia-myalgia from a contaminated product. Europe PMC: adult sleep work is cat/rat studies plus a 1981 case letter; the only sleep RCT is Bruni 2004 in children with sleep terrors (2 mg/kg, positive) - different population and outcome. Mood: Shaw 2002 Cochrane, 108 trials found, only 2 (n=64) met quality, inconclusive; Javelle 2020 Nutr Rev meta (13 studies, weak, few placebo-controlled) seen in listing. Sertraline + 5-HTP serotonin syndrome case (Am J Case Rep 2017) seen in search only. Safety: never-suggest on antidepressants. Price estimate (~$10-20/month).

safety.note: With SSRIs, MAOIs, tricyclics or linezolid, 5-HTP can push serotonin too high. A prescriber is the right person to ask.
5-HTP acts on serotonin, and mania has been reported. With bipolar disorder or ongoing mood care, start with a clinician.

items.name: Magnesium L-threonate (Magtein)
items.evidenceFor: better sleep from the threonate form specifically
items.evidenceSummary: Two trials, both paid for by makers of the Magtein form, found modest gains in self-rated sleep. Ring-tracked sleep improved in one and not the other.
items.doseTypical: 1 to 2 g product (about 75 to 145 mg magnesium)
items.humanQuestion: Did you pick this form for sleep or memory?
items.originQuestion: What drew you to this form of magnesium?
items.fitsInstead: If magnesium is the goal, plain glycinate at bedtime, though its sleep evidence is thin too.
items.notesInternal: Tier N by the brand-funding rule. Hausenblas 2024 Sleep Med X (full text): n=80, 1 g/day Magtein x21 days; funded by AIDP Inc. (3 authors are AIDP; product from Threotech); ISI interaction not significant (p=0.39); Oura deep/REM scores and some self-reports better. Europe PMC lists the grant as 'CNY Arts' - conflicts with the paper's own funding line; the paper says AIDP. There is a 2025 erratum. Lopresti 2025 Front Nutr (full text): n=100, 2 g/day (145 mg elemental) x6 weeks, funded by Threotech, which also co-designed the study; only PROMIS sleep-related impairment improved (p=0.043), Oura sleep unchanged; cognition composite improved. V3's 'Neurocentria' funding claim was not confirmed: funders are AIDP and Threotech. Plain magnesium has its own C-level sleep evidence (existing sources arab-2023, mah-2021, schuster-2025 - not re-opened here). Kidney safety row added from general magnesium knowledge plus MedlinePlus magnesium oxide precaution; NIH ODS page returned 403, so no fact-sheet citation. Price estimate (~$30-45/month for 2 g/day); vendor pages returned 403. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: With reduced kidney function, magnesium can build up in the blood. A clinician can say what amount is safe.

items.name: Magnesium spray or oil (on the skin)
items.evidenceFor: raising magnesium or better sleep through the skin
items.evidenceSummary: No controlled study shows magnesium crosses skin in meaningful amounts, and none has tested sleep. A 2017 review found the claims unsupported.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the evening rub you'd miss?
items.originQuestion: Where did you pick up the magnesium spray?
items.fitsInstead: A warm bath, or a magnesium glycinate capsule if the magnesium matters.
items.notesInternal: Tier N. Groeber 2017 Nutrients review (abstract via Europe PMC): claims that transdermal magnesium beats oral are not supported by scientific evidence; oral magnesium's benefits for deficiency are documented. Note: Groeber/Vormann are linked to magnesium-industry bodies, but the conclusion runs against the transdermal products. Found no sleep trial of magnesium spray. kind set to 'topical' (V3 said supplement). FORM_NOT_ABSORBED fits the core claim. Overlap: this key is NOT yet in the 'magnesium' group in existing-overlaps.json; needs adding or drop OVERLAP. fits_instead mentions a warm bath (evening warm bath has its own evidence row, haghayegh-2019). Price estimate (~$10-15 a bottle lasting about a month).

items.name: Chamomile tea
items.evidenceFor: sleep quality in adults
items.evidenceSummary: A 2024 review of 10 trials found better sleep-quality scores and fewer night wakings, mostly with extracts. Sleep length did not clearly change.
items.humanQuestion: Is the cup part of your wind-down?
items.notesInternal: Tier C. Kazemi 2024 Complement Ther Med meta-analysis (abstract): 10 trials, n=772 adults (healthy or with conditions); PSQI WMD -1.88 (CI -3.46 to -0.31, I2 88%) from 5 studies; fewer awakenings, no clear change in duration, efficiency or daytime function. Hieu 2019 Phytother Res: sleep quality SMD -0.73; one insomnia trial null. NCCIH 2024: very little info on insomnia; likely safe as tea; ragweed-family allergy; warfarin interaction. 'Mostly extracts' is my inference from the MeSH 'Plant Extracts' tag and the trials I know of; abstract didn't split tea vs extract, so flag. Ritual role anchor: the cup itself can carry the evening moment. Cheap, so UNUSED rarely matters. Price estimate (~$5-8 for a month of bags).

safety.note: Chamomile may interact with warfarin and some other medicines. A quick pharmacist check is worth it.
With a ragweed, daisy or chrysanthemum allergy, chamomile can set it off too.

items.name: Kombucha and probiotic drinks
items.evidenceFor: better gut health or digestion in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: A 2019 review found one human study. Newer trials are small and short; one in 90 healthy runners found no change in its main measure.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the fizzy afternoon drink you'd miss?
items.fitsInstead: Sparkling water with a splash of juice keeps the fizz.
items.notesInternal: Tier C, up from V3's D: Kapp & Sumner 2019 systematic review (Ann Epidemiol) found only one human study as of 2018, but small RCTs have appeared since: Arce-Lopez 2025 (n=58 healthy, 6 wk, fiber-enriched kombucha; triglycerides and Bifidobacterium shifted vs unfermented tea), Bonifacio 2026 (n=90 healthy beginner runners, 12 wk; primary outcome FRAP unchanged, other changes exploratory after FDR), Bonifacio 2026 second trial (n=59 overweight on calorie restriction; no between-group differences overall). Small, short, mixed = C. No kombucha-company funding disclosed in these records (public Brazilian/Spanish funders). 'Probiotic drinks' with named strains (e.g. Yakult-type for antibiotic diarrhoea) were not assessed here; if Veer wants them separate, they need their own row. Price: estimate. Search-result listings (ShopRite) showed GT's Synergy 16 oz at $3.99 to $4.49 regular; about 3 bottles a week is roughly $50/month. Safety row from TTB page: kombucha can ferment in the bottle to 0.5% ABV or more. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Kombucha can keep fermenting in the bottle, and some reaches 0.5% alcohol or more.

items.name: Matcha or green tea in the afternoon
items.evidenceFor: shorter sleep when afternoon caffeine lands within about nine hours of bed
items.evidenceSummary: A 2 g matcha serving holds roughly 60 to 80 mg of caffeine. Across 24 studies, caffeine shortened sleep; a 107 mg coffee needed about nine hours before bed.
items.doseTypical: about 60 to 80 caffeine per 2 g serving
items.humanQuestion: What time does the afternoon matcha usually happen?
items.fitsInstead: Move it earlier, or pour a caffeine-free tea for the afternoon pause.
items.notesInternal: Framed as a cost habit (sleep), so UNLOVED_HABIT and no EVIDENCE_REGULAR. Tier B, not A: the caffeine-sleep meta-analysis (Gardiner 2023, 24 studies, TST -45 min, coffee 107 mg needs >=8.8 h before bed) is strong for caffeine, but matcha itself was not tested and its dose is lower. Caffeine content from Unno 2026 review tables: 31 to 40 mg caffeine per g of matcha; I assumed a 2 g serving (common cafe/ceremonial serving; not from a source). Theanine + caffeine improved attention in small human studies cited by Unno; whether theanine softens the sleep cost is untested, so I did not claim it. Drake 2013: 400 mg even 6 h before bed disrupted sleep (higher dose than matcha). Whether the cost applies depends on bedtime: a 1pm matcha with an 11pm bed is outside the window, so the engine should pair this with a bedtime when it has one. Cost $30: estimate for a home matcha tin (cafe matcha would be far more).

safety.note: In pregnancy or while breastfeeding, a caffeine limit is worth checking with your clinician.

items.name: Bone broth
items.evidenceFor: skin, joint or gut health in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: No trials yet test bone broth for skin, joints or gut. Lab tests found fewer collagen building blocks than supplement doses in research. Independent collagen trials showed no skin benefit.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the warm mug you'd miss?
items.originQuestion: What got bone broth into your day?
items.fitsInstead: A mug of miso or homemade stock keeps the warmth.

swap.title: A mug of miso or homemade stock

items.notesInternal: Tier D: no human trials of bone broth for skin, joints or gut turned up in Europe PMC searches (bone broth + randomized/clinical trial/crossover). Alcock 2019 (IJSNEM, lab analysis): standardized-recipe broths had significantly lower glycine, proline, hydroxyproline etc. than a 20 g collagen supplement dose, with large variation across recipes; cafe broths highest. Alcock 2019 Front Nutr (300 mL broth in a plasma amino acid study) exists but I did not open it fully. Matar 2025 (Dig Dis Sci) is a narrative review arguing gut-barrier benefits from broth's components (glutamine, glycine), i.e. mechanism, not broth trials. Myung 2025 (existing source): collagen effects on skin vanish in non-industry-funded and high-quality RCTs, which undercuts the collagen rationale. It is a real food with some protein, so it is not harmful; D is about the borrowed claims. Price: estimate from search-result listings (Walmart $6.58, Thrive $7.99 for a 16.9 oz carton, about 2 mugs); a few mugs a week is about $50/month. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Hydrogen or alkaline water
items.evidenceFor: energy, recovery or general health in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: Hydrogen water trials are small and early; one meta-analysis found only small cholesterol changes in people with overweight. Claims that alkaline water changes body pH lack clinical support.
items.humanQuestion: Do you notice a difference from plain water?
items.fitsInstead: Plain tap or filtered water, in a bottle you like carrying.
items.notesInternal: Tier C (V3 said D). Hydrogen: Dhillon 2024 systematic review (25 studies, mixed designs) calls results preliminary and asks for larger, rigorous trials; Ye 2026 meta-analysis (13 RCTs, n=757, adults with BMI >=25, mostly cardiometabolic disease) found small TC/LDL drops below clinically meaningful thresholds and says it should not justify routine use. Small single trials in athletes (e.g. Chen 2026, n=13 crossover) report performance effects. That is small/short/mixed, so C rather than D. Alkaline: Alebrahim 2026 narrative review: some reflux (pepsin) and hydration-marker effects, mostly from mineral content; systemic alkalinization and anti-aging claims unsupported; caution in kidney disease. V3's claim that hydrogen trials are all seller-funded: I could not check funding statements from the abstracts, so I did not repeat it. The 'stomach acid neutralises it' line also isn't in what I opened, so it's left out. Price: estimate (bottled alkaline water or hydrogen tablets/cans run roughly $1 to $3 a day; generator bottles are a one-off $50 to $200).

safety.note: Alkaline and mineral waters carry extra minerals. With kidney disease, check with your clinician first.

items.name: Apple cider vinegar (shots or gummies)
items.evidenceFor: weight and blood sugar in adults without diabetes
items.evidenceSummary: Small trials, mostly in people with diabetes or overweight, show modest drops in blood sugar and weight. One headline weight trial was retracted in 2025.
items.doseTypical: 1 to 2 tablespoons (15 to 30 mL), diluted, before meals
items.humanQuestion: Is it the morning shot itself you'd miss?
items.fitsInstead: Vinegar on a salad at lunch, no shot needed.
items.notesInternal: Tier C for healthy 22 to 35 year olds. Shahmohammadi 2026 umbrella (10 meta-analyses, 38 RCTs): FBG -9.4 mg/dL, PPG -14.6, HbA1c -0.70%, weight -1.06 kg (rated high certainty), SBP -2.9; most trials in T2D/overweight, 8 in healthy people; over half poorly blinded. Arjmandfard 2025 (7 trials, T2D): FBS -21.9 mg/dL, HbA1c -1.53. Castagna 2025 (10 RCTs, n=789 overweight/T2D): SMD weight -0.39, BMI -0.65, trials 4 to 12 weeks. IMPORTANT: both Castagna and the umbrella's reference list include Abou-Khalil 2024 (BMJ Nutr Prev Health, Lebanese adolescents/young adults, n=120), which Europe PMC marks as a retracted publication (retraction 2025, doi 10.1136/bmjnph-2023-000823ret). That trial reported the largest weight effects and was the viral one, so the pooled weight estimates are inflated by an unknown amount. In people with T2D the glycaemic evidence is closer to B; there's no evidence_requires code for a diagnosis, so I kept C and put a diabetes safety row. Enamel: Willershausen 2014 in vitro, vinegars caused up to about 20% mineral loss in enamel at 4 h (raspberry vinegar); the umbrella authors also flag dental erosion, reflux, and caution with CKD and glucose/potassium-altering drugs. V3's 'Khezri 2018 n=39' is in Castagna's included list (not opened separately). Price: estimate; a 32 oz bottle of Bragg runs about $6 to $10 and lasts over a month at 1 tbsp/day; gummies cost more ($15 to $20).

safety.note: Vinegar softens tooth enamel. Dilute it well and rinse with plain water after.
On blood sugar medication, check with your clinician first; vinegar may add to the lowering effect.
With kidney disease, or on medicines that change potassium, check with your clinician before a daily habit.

items.name: Second (or third) coffee
items.evidenceFor: shorter, lighter sleep when the extra cup lands within about nine hours of bed
items.evidenceSummary: Across 24 studies, caffeine cut about 45 minutes of sleep, and a 107 mg coffee needed about nine hours before bed. FDA calls up to 400 mg a day generally fine for healthy adults.
items.humanQuestion: When does the last cup usually happen?
items.fitsInstead: Half-caf or decaf for the later cup keeps the ritual.
items.notesInternal: Cost habit, so UNLOVED_HABIT and no EVIDENCE_REGULAR. Tier A describes the cost of late caffeine: Gardiner 2023 meta-analysis (24 studies): TST -45 min, sleep efficiency -7%, SOL +9 min, WASO +12 min, less deep sleep; coffee (107 mg/250 mL) >=8.8 h before bed to avoid TST loss. Drake 2013 RCT: 400 mg at 0, 3 or 6 h before bed all disrupted sleep. FDA consumer page: 400 mg/day (about two to three 12 oz cups) generally not linked to negative effects in most adults; 12 oz brewed coffee is 113 to 247 mg. So a second cup at 10am is usually fine; the cost is timing or a total well past 400 mg. V3's HRV claim was not checked here and is left out. Cost $40 is an estimate (mix of home brew and some cafe cups); timing rows otherwise have no product cost. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: In pregnancy or while breastfeeding, a caffeine limit is worth checking with your clinician.

items.name: Fasting window or skipping breakfast
items.evidenceFor: weight loss in adults
items.evidenceSummary: Across 99 trials, time-restricted eating lowered weight versus eating freely, about as much as steady calorie cutting. Most trials included people with health conditions.
items.humanQuestion: Does the morning without food feel good to you?
items.notesInternal: Tier B for weight: Semnani-Azad 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis (99 RCTs, 6582 adults, only 720 healthy): every IF strategy and continuous calorie restriction beat ad-libitum eating for weight; vs calorie restriction only alternate-day fasting showed an edge (-1.29 kg, moderate certainty); time-restricted eating raised TC/LDL slightly vs whole-day fasting. B not A because most participants had health conditions and differences between strategies are small. It is a benefit row, so EVIDENCE_REGULAR; it's free, so nothing to clear. V3's claims about sleep/HRV effects and 'a week to adjust' were not checked and are left out of person-facing text. Safety rows (eating disorder history, diabetes medication, pregnancy) are standard clinical cautions, not from the BMJ paper; Veer may want a source for them.

safety.note: With a history of disordered eating, fasting windows are not a fit here.
On diabetes medication, long gaps without food can drop blood sugar. Check with your clinician first.
In pregnancy, check with your clinician before a fasting window.

items.name: Water filter (pitcher, faucet or under-sink)
items.evidenceFor: health benefit from filtering tap water at home
items.evidenceSummary: Certified faucet filters cut lead to low levels in field tests. CDC notes that if tap water has no harmful germs or chemicals, a filter may not be needed.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the taste, or something in your water?
items.fitsInstead: Testing your own tap first, since lead often comes from home pipes.
items.notesInternal: Tier C, and deliberately no BORROWED_WEAK even though C allows it: whether a filter matters depends on the home's water (lead service lines, old buildings, private wells, PFAS), which Distill can't see, so a 'let it go' could be wrong in exactly the homes where it matters. Only UNUSED (a filter that isn't changed or used). Evidence: CDC 2024 page: test first; if water has no harmful germs/chemicals a filter may not be needed; pitcher filters are mainly for taste and smell, may remove lead; check NSF standard on label. Purchase 2025 field test: lead-certified faucet filters brought occupied-home lead below 1 ug/L; a disturbed lead line overwhelmed them; iron clogged them. Hazzazi 2025: nine popular pitchers varied widely in mineral changes; none fully removed fluoride despite three makers' claims. No health-outcome trials of filtering already-compliant water exist that I found. Price: brita.com lists Elite replacement $19.99 and Original 1-pack $7.99; filter life not shown on the page I opened, so $5/month is an estimate. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: With lead pipes, an older building or a private well, test the water; a certified filter may matter.

items.name: Dessert or sweets right before bed
items.evidenceFor: lighter, more broken sleep when sweets come within an hour of bed
items.evidenceSummary: Eating within an hour of bed was linked to more night waking. A small study tied more daily sugar to more night arousals. Most of this is observed, not tested.
studiedForms: eating or drinking within 1 to 3 hours of bed
items.humanQuestion: Is the late dessert a want, or a habit?
items.fitsInstead: Dessert right after dinner keeps the sweet, with more time before bed.
items.notesInternal: Cost habit: UNLOVED_HABIT, no EVIDENCE_REGULAR. Tier C because the evidence is mostly observational: Iao 2022 (American Time Use Survey, nationally representative): eating/drinking <1 h before bed linked to longer sleep but about 2 to 2.6x the odds of WASO >30 min; causality unclear. St-Onge 2016 (26 adults, inpatient crossover; diet-sleep link analysed by regression on one ad-libitum day): higher % energy from sugar associated with more arousals; low fibre/high sat fat with lighter sleep. Kesgin 2025 (16 healthy 18 to 35 y, 1-week crossover): eating >=25% of calories after 9:30pm raised AHI and lowered melatonin; that's heavy late eating, not a small dessert, so I used it as support only. No trial isolates a bedtime dessert. Cost 0: part of groceries. A loved evening ritual stays (THEIRS, LOVED).

items.name: Chlorophyll water (liquid chlorophyll drops)
items.evidenceFor: clearer skin, energy or less bloating in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: Skin evidence is two ten-person studies of gels, not drinks. No trials yet test chlorophyll water for energy or bloating. Most drops are chlorophyllin, a copper-based form.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the green morning glass you'd miss?
items.originQuestion: Where did chlorophyll water first show up for you?
items.fitsInstead: A glass of water with a handful of spinach in a smoothie.
items.notesInternal: Tier D: Linus Pauling Institute (Oregon State) chlorophyll/chlorophyllin page (updated 2021, reviewed 2022): most OTC 'chlorophyll' is sodium copper chlorophyllin; skin evidence is two 10-person topical gel pilots (acne, photodamage) plus case reports; odor-control evidence mixed (one placebo-controlled colostomy trial null); the aflatoxin-adduct RCT (n=180, China) is in a high-exposure population and irrelevant here. No oral trials for skin, energy or bloating turned up in Europe PMC searches. LPI: not tested in pregnancy or lactation; green stools, tongue discoloration, false-positive guaiac test. Dose shown is what odor studies used, not a benefit threshold. Price: estimate ($12 to $20 a bottle lasting about a month).

safety.note: Chlorophyll supplements have not been tested in pregnancy.
Chlorophyll supplements have not been tested while breastfeeding.

items.name: Activated charcoal (capsules)
items.evidenceFor: less gas and bloating in healthy adults
items.evidenceSummary: Charcoal binds drugs in the gut, which is why emergency rooms use it after overdoses. For everyday gas, small trials mostly found no effect. It binds your medicines too.
studiedForms: activated charcoal 400 mg twice daily to 0.52 g four times daily in gas studies
items.humanQuestion: What do you reach for it for?
items.notesInternal: V3 graded N with a 'no detox to do' line; I've avoided that word in person-facing text. Tier C for gas/bloating because small human trials exist and mostly found nothing: Suarez 1999 (5 healthy volunteers, 0.52 g x4/day for 1 wk; no change in fecal sulfur gases, total gas or symptoms); Di Stefano 2000 RCT (34 functional patients; charcoal 400 mg bid did not lower breath H2 or symptoms, rifaximin did). A gastroenterologist quoted in a CU Anschutz news piece (search snippet only, not opened) says 1980s studies split. The popular 'cleanse' and hangover claims have no human studies I could find (effectively N). Juurlink 2016 (Br J Clin Pharmacol review): single-dose charcoal reduces absorption of many drugs; clinical overdose use. Elomaa 2001 (11 women, pill users): charcoal taken 3 h after and >=12 h before the pill did not cause ovulation. That timing is the basis for the safety note. Price: estimate ($10 to $15 a bottle).

safety.note: Charcoal binds many medicines, including the pill. Take it at least 3 hours after or 12 hours before, and ask a pharmacist.

items.name: LED face mask (red and near-infrared light)
items.evidenceFor: softer fine lines with regular home use
items.evidenceSummary: Small trials, several maker-funded, found red and near-infrared light softened fine lines. Home masks are weaker than clinic lights. For mild acne, six trials found fewer spots.
studiedForms: clinic panels in most wrinkle trials
items.humanQuestion: Is it more for fine lines or breakouts?
items.fitsInstead: Daily sunscreen and a nightly retinoid carry stronger evidence for fine lines.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded B; downgraded to C for fine lines. The best wrinkle RCT (Lee 2007, n=76, sham, double-blind, abstract only) used clinic LEDs twice weekly for 4 weeks, not a home mask, and is single-centre; Wunsch 2014 (full text) was fully sponsor-funded with a non-randomized control group drawn mainly from sponsor staff. Bu 2024 and Grimes 2025 (both full text) call home-device evidence limited/mixed; only a third of LED studies had a control plus blinding. AAD (2024) says home devices are hard to judge. ACNE IS DIFFERENT: Ershadi 2025 JAMA Derm meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (216 people) found ~45% greater lesion reduction with home red/blue LED, 4 of 6 low risk of bias; that is B-level for mild to moderate acne. If Veer/Ishan want a split row (acne vs aging), acne would be B with EVIDENCE_REGULAR. The human_question asks which goal so the engine does not clear an acne user on the aging tier. Price: CurrentBody Series 3 $569.99 (opened); Omnilux and others are similar or lower; spread over 24 months about $20 to $24. Cadence daily approximates the 3 to 5 sessions a week on the label. fits_instead rests on existing A rows (sunscreen-daily-spf-30, retinol-retinoid-nightly). Layne 2026 abstract only; its author declares device-company honoraria.

safety.note: Some medicines, like certain antibiotics, make skin more sensitive to light. A pharmacist or clinician can say whether an LED mask is fine.
Acne that has not settled after a few months, or light-sensitive skin such as lupus, is worth a dermatologist visit before starting.
Makers say masks have not been tested in pregnancy, so it is worth asking a clinician first.
Makers say masks have not been tested while breastfeeding, so it is worth asking a clinician first.

items.name: Gua sha or ice roller (facial)
items.evidenceFor: a less puffy, more contoured-looking face
items.evidenceSummary: In a small eight-week trial, gua sha and a facial roller both slightly reshaped facial contours, with no untouched comparison group. A roller briefly raises blood flow.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the cool morning minute you enjoy?
items.fitsInstead: A cool spoon or cold cloth in the morning gives the same chill.
items.notesInternal: Kept at C (V3 C), but it is a soft C: Ahn 2025 (n=34, abstract) compared gua sha against a roller with no untreated arm, so the 2 to 3 mm contour change cannot be separated from measurement drift or water retention changes. Miyaji 2018 (abstract) shows only a short blood-flow rise, and one author is from MTG Co., a roller maker (marked brand_funded yes). No study found on ice rollers or cold for cosmetic de-puffing; V3's "de-puffing lasts hours" claim was not verified and is not in the summary. Hamp 2023 (J Cosmet Dermatol, "Gua-sha, jade roller, and facial massage") exists but has no abstract and the full text was blocked (403), so it is not cited. A stricter reader could call this D. Cost: about $20 to $30 one-off, spread over 24 months (estimate, no pricing page opened). also_serves mind because the appeal is mostly the calm ritual. No safety rows: none found in sources opened.

items.name: Microcurrent device (NuFACE and similar)
items.evidenceFor: a lifted, firmer-looking face
items.evidenceSummary: We found no independent trial of a NuFACE-style microcurrent device. A 2024 review called the research scarce, and the one trial it cited tested a different electrical device.
items.humanQuestion: Do you still use it most mornings?
items.originQuestion: How did the microcurrent device come into your routine?
items.fitsInstead: A two-minute face massage with moisturizer keeps the hands-on ritual.
items.notesInternal: Tier D (V3 D). PubMed search for microcurrent plus face/wrinkle returned no RCT of a NuFACE-type device. Bu 2024 (full text) says microcurrent research is relatively scarce; its only trial (Slendertone Face) is neuromuscular stimulation, not microcurrent. Other hits were combined RF-microcurrent devices run by contract labs or device teams (Nobile 2016, Kubik 2026), not the same technology, so not cited. Layne 2026 (abstract) is general about home devices. A 2026 Cutis letter (Kadam and Lipner) on adverse events from home microcurrent devices exists, but the full text was paywalled, so it is not cited; worth Ishan pulling. Price: NuFACE MINI+ $250, TRINITY+ $395 (opened), over 24 months plus conductive gel, about $20 (estimate for gel). Safety rows come from brand warnings via Space NK (opened).

safety.note: The maker says not to use it with a pacemaker or other implanted device. A clinician can advise.
The maker advises against use in pregnancy, since electrical stimulation has not been shown safe then.
The maker says it is not for anyone under 18.
The maker says to avoid inflamed or broken-out skin. Acne or rosacea that will not settle is worth a dermatologist visit.

items.name: Facials (monthly, at a spa or skin studio)
items.evidenceFor: smoother, clearer-looking skin
items.evidenceSummary: Little research tests regular spa facials. One small trial of six hydradermabrasion sessions, about a week apart, found fewer fine lines and smaller pores. Monthly visits are untested.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the hour of calm you would miss?
items.fitsInstead: A facial each season, with a simple daily routine between visits.
items.notesInternal: Tier C (V3 C). "Facial" covers many services; the only controlled study found was Freedman 2008 (n=20, abstract): six hydradermabrasion sessions 7 to 10 days apart beat hand-applied serum. That is weekly, not monthly, and a single plastic-surgery practice; funding not stated in the abstract (marked no, unverified). No trial of monthly spa facials found. V3's "no lasting change" was not tested directly. The calm/treat value is real and should carry it. Price: Heyday membership $95 to $105/month incl. one 50-minute facial (brand franchising page, opened); independent spas often charge more. UNUSED covers lapsed memberships. also_serves mind for the hour of calm.

safety.note: For acne that will not settle, eczema or rosacea, a dermatologist is a better first stop than a facial.

items.name: Eye cream (alongside a face moisturizer)
items.evidenceFor: more benefit around the eyes than the face moisturizer already gives
items.evidenceSummary: A 2024 review found few trials of eye creams themselves. Ingredients like retinoids and caffeine have small studies around the eyes, so the ingredient matters more than the jar.
studiedForms: peptide or hyaluronic acid eye creams
items.humanQuestion: Does it hold anything your moisturizer lacks?
items.originQuestion: Who recommended an eye cream on top of your moisturizer?
items.fitsInstead: Your moisturizer, patted gently around the eyes with the ring finger.
items.notesInternal: Tier D for the doubled step (V3 C). Hamie 2024 (abstract) names the lack of trials on eye cream formulations as a key limitation; individual ingredients have small studies. No trial compares an eye cream with the same user's face moisturizer around the eyes. Messaraa 2020 (Oriflame-run, n=49, abstract) found a five-step routine incl. eye cream beat a two-step one over 4 weeks, but it tests the whole routine and is brand-funded. V3's claim that most eye creams are the brand's moisturizer in a smaller jar was NOT verified and is left out. AAD (opened) warns too many products can irritate and suggests the ring finger near the eyes; fits_instead leans on that. Keep if it carries a retinoid or caffeine the moisturizer lacks: the human_question surfaces that. Price $45/month is V3's estimate, not checked; drugstore eye creams cost far less. Moisturizer near the eyes being fine is a reasonable inference, not an explicit AAD statement.

items.name: Toner (hydrating or balancing)
items.evidenceFor: more hydration when a moisturizer is already used
items.evidenceSummary: In a small study, toner then cream hydrated skin about as well as cream alone. The AAD advises skipping toners with rosacea.
items.humanQuestion: Does skin feel different on days you skip it?
items.originQuestion: Where did toner come into your routine from?
items.fitsInstead: Moisturizer straight after cleansing, while skin is still a little damp.
items.notesInternal: Tier D (V3 N). Yuanxi 2016 (abstract, sample size not stated in abstract) is the only direct test found: cream alone matched toner plus cream on dry skin; toner alone ranked last; re-applying toner every 2 h did add hydration. Messaraa 2020 (brand-run) tests a whole routine. AAD rosacea page (existing source) says never use astringents or toners with rosacea; AAD order page and 2025 guide favor fewer products. V3's claim that modern cleansers do not leave skin needing rebalancing was not verified and is left out. Exfoliating (acid) toners are a different product and belong with the exfoliant rows. Damp-skin tip in fits_instead leans on the existing aad-2026-dry-skin source (Veer to confirm wording there). Price $25 is V3's estimate.

safety.note: With rosacea, the AAD advises skipping toners and astringents. A dermatologist can suggest a gentler routine.

items.name: Facial plus at-home LED plus microcurrent (all three)
items.evidenceFor: more visible change from all three than from one alone
items.evidenceSummary: No study tests stacking all three. Home LED has small trials for fine lines, monthly facials are untested, and microcurrent devices have almost no independent research.
items.humanQuestion: Which of the three would you keep first?
items.originQuestion: How did a facial, LED and microcurrent all end up in your routine?
items.fitsInstead: The one you would keep, plus daily sunscreen.
items.notesInternal: Tier D for the stack (V3 C). No study of combining facials, home LED and microcurrent was found; each part is graded in its own row (LED C, facials C, microcurrent D). TOO_MANY_STEPS fits: AAD warns many products and multiple anti-aging steps can irritate, though devices are not products, so this is a stretch Veer may want to drop. kind set to device because two of three parts are devices; there is no combo kind. Cost: Heyday ~$100 + LED ~$20 + microcurrent ~$20 = ~$140 (V3 had $200). Cadence weekly is a blend: facial monthly, devices most days. fits_instead rests on the sunscreen A row.

items.name: Red light therapy panel (at home)
items.evidenceFor: softer fine lines and smoother skin
items.evidenceSummary: One maker-funded trial of full-body red light found smoother skin and softer lines. Recovery evidence comes from lights placed on muscles, and the sleep study had twenty athletes.
items.doseTypical: 10 to 20 minutes, several times a week
items.humanQuestion: Is it mostly for skin, or for recovery?
items.notesInternal: Tier C for skin (V3 C). Wunsch 2014 (full text) is the closest match to a panel (full-body units) and found gains vs untreated controls, but was fully sponsor-funded with non-randomized, sponsor-employee controls and no sham. AAD 2024 (full text) supports subtle-to-noticeable results for aging skin but says home devices are hard to judge. Recovery: Dutra 2022 meta-analysis (abstract) found small gains in single-joint endurance and cycling time to exhaustion, none in strength or running; trials used lasers/LED clusters on muscles pre-exercise, not panels, so the move claim is C at best. Sleep: Zhao 2012 (abstract) is 20 athletes, not blinded; D for sleep. V3 testosterone claim rests on rat data; not searched further and left out. Price: Mito panels $249 to $749 for most home sizes (brand page, opened), over 24 months about $10 to $31; used $20. fits_instead points to morning-sunlight-10-min-outdoors (a different benefit, circadian, not skin); Veer may prefer "". Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

safety.note: Some medicines make skin more sensitive to light. A pharmacist or clinician can say whether a red light panel is fine.
Light-sensitive skin, such as lupus, can flare with light, so a dermatologist visit comes first.

items.name: Hair growth gummies (biotin blends, such as SugarBearHair)
items.evidenceFor: fuller, faster-growing hair without a deficiency
items.evidenceSummary: No study we found tests these gummies. A review found biotin helped hair only when an underlying cause like deficiency was present, and deficiency is uncommon.
items.humanQuestion: Have you noticed any change in your hair?
items.originQuestion: Where did you first see the hair gummies?
items.fitsInstead: A dermatologist visit, if hair shedding is the real worry.
items.notesInternal: Tier N for mass-market biotin gummies (V3 N). Patel 2017 (full text): every case of biotin helping hair had an underlying condition; no RCTs in healthy people. ConsumerLab (opened): SugarBearHair is 5,000 mcg biotin per 2 gummies, ~$30 for 60, no studies of the formula, and over-labeled vitamin amounts. Drake 2023 JAMA Derm review (abstract): some branded multi-ingredient products (Viviscal, Nutrafol, Lamdapil, Pantogar) showed potential benefit, mostly in company-run trials. If a user has one of those, a separate row may be warranted (likely C), so this row should not be matched to Nutrafol/Viviscal. These gummies also hold a multivitamin's worth of A, B, C, D, E: Veer may want this key added to the existing daily-multivitamin group (only new groups go in overlap_additions, so not done here). Lab-test interference from Li 2017 and FDA (opened) drives the safety note. Price $30/month from ConsumerLab (opened).

safety.note: These gummies hold biotin, which can skew some blood tests, including a heart test. Mention them before any blood draw.
Sudden, patchy or heavy hair shedding is worth a dermatologist visit, since it often has a cause worth finding.

items.name: Biotin (vitamin B7) supplement
items.evidenceFor: hair or nail growth
items.evidenceSummary: Biotin helped hair and nails in rare cases of deficiency or specific conditions. No trial shows a benefit for healthy people, and typical diets already cover it.
items.humanQuestion: Did a clinician suggest it, or a friend?
items.fitsInstead: A clinician check, if hair or nails have changed lately.
items.notesInternal: V3 N; here C with evidence_requires deficiency, tier_otherwise N. Patel 2017 (full text): 18 published cases, all with an underlying cause (inherited biotinidase or holocarboxylase deficiency, uncombable hair, brittle nails, valproate use), all improved; this is case-report evidence, so C, not B, even for the deficient. No RCT in healthy people. Adult AI is 30 mcg; Western diets give about 35 to 70 mcg (Patel). NIH ODS biotin fact sheets returned 403 to both WebFetch and curl, so not cited; worth re-checking (they also discuss lab interference and anticonvulsant-related low biotin). Lab interference: Li 2017 (abstract) 10 mg/day for a week skewed 9 of 23 biotin-based assays incl. thyroid; FDA troponin page (opened, current as of 2022) reports falsely low troponin. The FDA consumer safety communication URL 404d; not cited. Cost $8 is V3's, not checked. Area skin since the use is hair and nails; no hair area exists.

safety.note: Biotin can skew some blood tests, including a heart test. Mention it before any blood draw.
Sudden, patchy or heavy hair shedding is worth a dermatologist visit, since it often has a cause worth finding.

items.name: Collagen drinks and beauty gummies
items.evidenceFor: firmer, more hydrated skin
items.evidenceSummary: Trials paid for by collagen makers found small gains in skin hydration and elasticity. Independent, higher-quality trials found no clear difference. One positive trial used 2.5 g daily.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the drink you enjoy, or the skin goal?
items.fitsInstead: Daily sunscreen, which slowed skin aging over four years in one trial.
items.notesInternal: V3 graded B; set to C to match the reviewed collagen-peptides row (same evidence: Myung 2025, de Miranda 2021, Proksch 2014, all reused by id). V3's claim that gummies and drinks carry a fraction of the dose is only partly true: Vital Proteins gummies list 2.5 g VERISOL per serving at $16.99 for 30 servings (opened), which matches the Proksch dose. Other gummies list far less (a Walmart listing showed 120 mg, but the page was bot-blocked, so not cited); DOSE_BELOW_MIN handles those case by case. Cost $25 is an estimate between gummies (~$17) and ready-to-drink shots (not priced here). Area skin rather than eat because these are sold as beauty products; collagen-peptides sits in eat with also_serves skin.

items.name: Class pack or studio credits
items.evidenceFor: aerobic fitness and strength, from the classes taken
items.evidenceSummary: Regular classes build fitness like any training. The benefit lives in the classes taken.
items.humanQuestion: How many credits are left before the pack expires?
items.notesInternal: V3 graded A off an unsourced claim that unused credits are the most common wellness purchase that does nothing; I found no study of class-pack or ClassPass breakage, so that claim is dropped. The A now belongs to the training (HIIT trials, WHO activity guidance), held only for people who use it (trains, otherwise N), matching gym-membership and boutique rows. Usage evidence is DellaVigna and Malmendier 2006 (gym memberships, not packs). Expiry matters: SoulCycle's opened series page (San Francisco) lists 5 classes $185 (45-day expiry), 10 for $365 (3 months), 20 for $710 (9 months). cost_month_usd 120 = a 10-pack spread over its 3-month expiry. ClassPass official pricing page returned 403; third-party summaries show $19 for 8 credits up to about $139 to $159, with rollover capped, so not used for the price. Clear codes follow the gym rows (UNUSED, OVERLAP), not BORROWED_WEAK. Validation 24 Oct: edited per the independent re-check (data/validation).

items.name: Massage membership (Massage Envy, Squeeze)
items.evidenceFor: lower anxiety and less muscle soreness after sessions
items.evidenceSummary: A 2004 review of 37 trials found one massage eases anxiety, heart rate and blood pressure, and a course eases lasting anxiety. Massage also ranks top for post-workout soreness.
items.humanQuestion: Are the monthly massages getting booked, or banking up?
items.fitsInstead: Pay per massage in the months you want one.
items.notesInternal: V3 B kept. Moyer, Rounds and Hannum 2004 (Psychol Bull, 37 randomised studies, mixed healthy and clinical samples): single sessions lowered state anxiety, BP and heart rate but not cortisol, negative mood or immediate pain; multiple sessions lowered delayed pain, trait anxiety and depression. Dupuy 2018 (Front Physiol meta-analysis, post-exercise recovery) found massage the most effective technique for DOMS and perceived fatigue, single sessions only. B not A because samples are mixed and old, and effects are mostly short-term. V3's 'HRV goes up' not verified, dropped. Prices opened: ThePricer (updated Aug 2026) puts Massage Envy membership at about $70 to $90 a month for one 60-min session, 12-month initial term; unused benefits accrue but are forfeited 60 days after cancelling. Squeeze (Fort Worth opening article, Mar 2024): $95 a month for 50 min, $125 for 80 min, credits roll over and never expire, cancel anytime. cost 90 is the midpoint. Massage Envy's own page returned empty.

safety.note: Rare clots and nerve injuries follow vigorous massage. With a clotting or bleeding condition, or on blood thinners, a clinician check comes first.

items.name: Sauna or bathhouse membership
items.evidenceFor: heart and blood vessel health over the long run
items.evidenceSummary: A Finnish study of men over about 20 years links frequent sauna use with fewer heart deaths; trials are few and small. A membership pays off in the visits made.
items.humanQuestion: Is it the heat, or the people you go with?
items.fitsInstead: A gym with a sauna, or a hot bath at home.
items.notesInternal: V3 B changed to C to match the reviewed sauna row (sauna-post-workout-or-evening), which reused the same sources: one observational cohort of Finnish men (Laukkanen 2015) plus small trials. No new sources needed. Price opened: Bathhouse (abathhouse.com, NYC: Atlantic Ave, Flatiron, Williamsburg) Starter $145 a month for 3 day passes, Standard $225 for 5. Othership's membership page lists rollover of unused credits but showed no prices. Safety rows mirror the sauna row. V3 typical 2 to 4 visits a week kept as dose_typical; the cohort's clearest links were at 4 to 7.

safety.note: Unstable chest pain, a recent heart attack or a severely narrowed aortic valve call for a clinician's go-ahead first.
Heat lowers blood pressure for a while, so with low blood pressure or blood pressure medicines, check with a clinician.
Saunas are considered safe in a healthy, uncomplicated pregnancy, though a clinician check first is wise.

items.name: Recovery studio membership (Restore, Remedy Place, Othership)
items.evidenceFor: less muscle soreness after hard exercise (cold water, compression, massage)
items.evidenceSummary: Cold plunges, compression and contrast baths ease soreness a little after hard training. Whole-body cryo and IV drips lack good trials. Sauna's heart link comes from one long Finnish study.
items.humanQuestion: Which room do you head to first?
items.fitsInstead: A pay-per-visit pass for the sauna and plunge you use.
items.notesInternal: V3 C restructured to match the cold-plunge row: B for soreness when the person trains (Dupuy 2018 meta-analysis: immersion, contrast water, compression and massage all cut DOMS; Machado 2016 and Moore 2022 for cold water), C otherwise (sauna heart evidence is a single cohort; mood claims thin). Add-ons: whole-body cryo insufficient per Cochrane (Costello 2015, 4 tiny RCTs); IV drips no evidence in healthy people (Merck Manual 2025). Prices opened: Athletech News (Sep 2024) Restore NYC tiers about $250 (8 services), $390 (14), $449 (31), 3-month minimum per directory listings (not opened); Boston Globe (Mar 2025) Remedy Place $450 to $3,250 a month; Time Out (2025) Remedy Place from $595. Othership pricing not shown on its pages. cost 250 = Restore entry tier; Remedy Place members sit far higher. Safety rows combine the sauna and cold-plunge rows.

safety.note: Cold shock and strong heat both strain the heart, so with a heart condition a clinician check comes first.
Cold pushes blood pressure up and heat drops it, so with high or low blood pressure, check with a clinician.
Check with a clinician before cold plunges, cryo or IV drips during pregnancy.

items.name: Second gym or studio membership
items.evidenceFor: strength and fitness, from the visits that happen
items.evidenceSummary: Training builds strength and fitness wherever it happens. A second membership adds something only when both get used.
items.humanQuestion: Which of the two did you go to more?
items.fitsInstead: Keep the one you use; drop-in passes cover the other.
