sources.citation: Hillman AR, Trickett O, Brodsky C, Chrismas B. Montmorency tart cherry supplementation does not impact sleep, body composition, cellular health, or blood pressure in healthy adults. Nutr Health. 2022 (online).
sources.finding: Thirty days of tart cherry juice or capsules did not change sleep time or quality versus placebo.

sources.citation: Tucker RM, Kim N, Gurzell E, et al. Commonly used dose of Montmorency tart cherry powder does not improve sleep or inflammation outcomes in individuals with overweight or obesity. Nutrients. 2024;16:4125.
sources.finding: 500 mg tart cherry capsules an hour before bed for two weeks changed no sleep or inflammation measure versus placebo.
sources.population: 34 adults with sleep complaints and overweight or obesity, crossover

sources.citation: Suraev AS, Marshall NS, Vandrey R, et al. Cannabinoid therapies in the management of sleep disorders: a systematic review of preclinical and clinical studies. Sleep Med Rev. 2020;53:101339.
sources.finding: Evidence is insufficient to support cannabinoids for any sleep disorder; studies were few, small and at moderate-to-high risk of bias.

sources.citation: Narayan AJ, Downey LA, Rose S, Di Natale L, Hayley AC. Cannabidiol for moderate-severe insomnia: a randomized controlled pilot trial of 150 mg of nightly dosing. J Clin Sleep Med. 2024;20(5):753-763.
sources.finding: 150 mg CBD nightly for two weeks matched placebo on insomnia severity and most sleep measures; well-being ratings were higher on CBD.

sources.citation: Bonn-Miller MO, Loflin MJE, Thomas BF, Marcu JP, Hyke T, Vandrey R. Labeling accuracy of cannabidiol extracts sold online. JAMA. 2017;318(17):1708-1709.
sources.finding: Of 84 CBD products bought online, 31% held CBD within 10% of the label; 43% held more, 26% less, and 21% contained THC.

sources.citation: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH). Cannabis (marijuana) and cannabinoids: what you need to know. Updated November 2019.
sources.finding: CBD interacts with other drugs and has been linked to liver injury; over-the-counter CBD may hold more or less than labeled, and may contain THC.

sources.citation: US Food and Drug Administration. What you should know about using cannabis, including CBD, when pregnant or breastfeeding. Consumer update, 16 October 2019.
sources.finding: FDA strongly advises against CBD, THC or marijuana in any form during pregnancy or breastfeeding; liver damage and drug interactions are known CBD risks.

sources.citation: Pittler MH, Ernst E. Kava extract for treating anxiety. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2003;(1):CD003383.
sources.finding: Across 11 trials, kava extract reduced anxiety scores more than placebo; short-term use of 1 to 24 weeks looked relatively safe, with mild side effects.

sources.citation: Sarris J, Byrne GJ, Bousman CA, et al. Kava for generalised anxiety disorder: a 16-week double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled study. Aust N Z J Psychiatry. 2020;54(3):288-297.
sources.finding: Kava at 240 mg kavalactones daily did no better than placebo for diagnosed anxiety over 16 weeks; liver test changes were more frequent on kava.
sources.population: 171 unmedicated adults with generalised anxiety disorder

sources.citation: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH). Kava. Updated April 2025.
sources.finding: Kava may ease anxiety but not generalized anxiety disorder; rare, sometimes serious liver injury reported; avoid with alcohol or sedatives; possible risks in pregnancy.

sources.citation: Teschke R, Schwarzenboeck A, Hennermann KH. Kava hepatotoxicity: a clinical survey and critical analysis of 26 suspected cases. Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2008.
sources.finding: Of 26 suspected kava liver injuries, eight showed possible or probable causality; overdose, long use and other medicines appeared to raise the risk.
sources.population: 26 patients with suspected kava liver injury

sources.citation: Viola H, Wasowski C, Levi de Stein M, et al. Apigenin, a component of Matricaria recutita flowers, is a central benzodiazepine receptors-ligand with anxiolytic effects. Planta Med. 1995;61(3):213-216.
sources.finding: Apigenin from chamomile bound benzodiazepine receptors and reduced anxiety-like behaviour in mice; only a tenfold higher dose caused mild sedation.

sources.citation: Mastrofini GF, Romersi RF, Lombardi MG, et al. Modulating stress and sleep through a multi-compound dietary supplement: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2026.
sources.finding: A morning adaptogen and evening blend improved perceived stress and sleep; the evening blend held 50 mg apigenin with magnesium threonate and theanine, so apigenin alone was untested.

sources.citation: Kazemi A, Shojaei-Zarghani S, Eskandarzadeh P, Hashempur MH. Effects of chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla L.) on sleep: a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical trials. Complement Ther Med. 2024;84:103071.
sources.finding: Chamomile improved sleep-quality scores and reduced night wakings; no clear change in sleep duration, efficiency or daytime function; heterogeneity was high.
sources.population: 10 clinical trials, 772 adults, healthy or with medical conditions

sources.citation: Hieu TH, Dibas M, Surya Dila KA, et al. Therapeutic efficacy and safety of chamomile for state anxiety, generalized anxiety disorder, insomnia, and sleep quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Phytother Res. 2019;33(6):1604-1615.
sources.finding: Chamomile improved sleep quality and generalized anxiety scores; the one insomnia trial showed no change; reported side effects were mild.

sources.citation: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH). Chamomile. Updated November 2024.
sources.finding: Very little evidence on chamomile for insomnia; likely safe as tea; allergy more likely with ragweed-family allergies; may interact with warfarin.

sources.citation: Boonstra E, de Kleijn R, Colzato LS, Alkemade A, Forstmann BU, Nieuwenhuis S. Neurotransmitters as food supplements: the effects of GABA on brain and behavior. Front Psychol. 2015;6:1520.
sources.finding: Whether swallowed GABA crosses the blood-brain barrier is unresolved; evidence for calming effects often came from researchers with potential conflicts of interest.
sources.population: Human and animal GABA supplement studies

sources.citation: Hepsomali P, Groeger JA, Nishihira J, Scholey A. Effects of oral gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) administration on stress and sleep in humans: a systematic review. Front Neurosci. 2020;14:923.
sources.finding: Across 14 placebo-controlled trials, oral GABA showed limited evidence for stress relief and very limited evidence for sleep benefits.

sources.citation: Shaw K, Turner J, Del Mar C. Tryptophan and 5-hydroxytryptophan for depression. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2002;(1):CD003198.
sources.finding: Of 108 trials, only two (64 people) met quality criteria; they hinted at benefit for depression but were too weak to conclude, and safety was unresolved.

sources.citation: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. About Herbs: 5-HTP. Updated 2 June 2022.
sources.finding: Studies of 5-HTP for insomnia are lacking; avoid with SSRIs, MAOIs or tricyclics without a physician because of serotonin syndrome risk.
sources.population: Review of human evidence and case reports

sources.citation: Bruni O, Ferri R, Miano S, Verrillo E. L-5-Hydroxytryptophan treatment of sleep terrors in children. Eur J Pediatr. 2004.
sources.finding: Bedtime 5-HTP for 20 days stopped sleep terrors in most treated children, versus under a third of the comparison group.

sources.citation: Lopresti AL, Smith SJ. The effects of magnesium L-threonate (Magtein) on cognitive performance and sleep quality in adults: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Front Nutr. 2025;12:1729164.
sources.finding: 2 g Magtein daily for six weeks improved one self-rated sleep measure and cognition scores; ring-measured sleep duration and stages did not change.
sources.population: 100 adults aged 18-45 with self-reported poor sleep

sources.citation: Kapp JM, Sumner W. Kombucha: a systematic review of the empirical evidence of human health benefit. Ann Epidemiol. 2019;30:66-70.
sources.finding: Searching databases and trial registries in 2018 across 310 articles found only one study reporting kombucha's effects in people.

sources.citation: Bonifacio DB, de Paulo RS, Mendes PHV, et al. Acute and chronic effects of green tea kombucha with and without grape skin extract on immune and oxidative stress markers in beginner runners: a randomized controlled trial. J Food Sci. 2026.
sources.finding: Twelve weeks of green tea kombucha did not change the main antioxidant measure; a few immune and oxidative changes were exploratory after correction.
sources.population: 90 healthy adults aged 18 to 45 starting running training

sources.citation: Arce-Lopez B, Bazan GX, Molina S, et al. Effect of fiber-modified kombucha tea on gut microbiota in healthy population: a randomized controlled trial. Curr Res Food Sci. 2025;11:101130.
sources.finding: Six weeks of 250 mL a day of fibre-enriched kombucha shifted triglycerides and raised Bifidobacterium versus unfermented tea; authors call for more trials.

sources.citation: Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau. Kombucha. ttb.gov (updated 13 Aug 2019).
sources.finding: Kombucha can reach 0.5% alcohol or more during production or after bottling, as fermentation can continue in the bottle.

sources.citation: Unno K, Kameoka Y, Nakamura Y. Compositional diversity and functional interactions of bioactive compounds in Japanese green tea: focus on matcha, sencha, and gyokuro. Molecules. 2026;31(16):2934.
sources.finding: Matcha samples held roughly 31 to 40 mg caffeine per gram plus theanine; small human studies found caffeine with theanine helped attention.
sources.population: Matcha and Japanese green tea samples; small human studies reviewed

sources.citation: Alcock RD, Shaw GC, Burke LM. Bone broth unlikely to provide reliable concentrations of collagen precursors compared with supplemental sources of collagen used in collagen research. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019.
sources.finding: Standard-recipe bone broths held significantly less glycine, proline and hydroxyproline than a 20 g collagen supplement dose, and recipes varied widely.
sources.population: Commercial, cafe and lab-made bone broth samples

sources.citation: Matar A, Abdelnaem N, Camilleri M. Bone broth benefits: how its nutrients fortify gut barrier in health and disease. Dig Dis Sci. 2025.
sources.finding: Narrative review arguing broth's amino acids and minerals may support the gut barrier, based on studies of the components rather than broth trials.
sources.population: Animal and human studies of broth components

sources.citation: Dhillon G, Buddhavarapu V, Grewal H, et al. Hydrogen water: extra healthy or a hoax? A systematic review. Int J Mol Sci. 2024;25(2):973.
sources.finding: Twenty-five studies of hydrogen-rich water showed early, encouraging signals; larger, more rigorous trials are needed before benefits can be confirmed.
sources.population: Mixed human studies (exercise, liver, mood, ageing and others)

sources.citation: Ye H, Fang J, Safargar M, Fareed H, Prabahar K, Jin P. The effect of hydrogen-rich water interventions on lipid profiles in adults with overweight or obesity and associated metabolic disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Diabetol Metab Syndr. 2026;18(1):114.
sources.finding: Across 13 RCTs, hydrogen-rich water slightly lowered total and LDL cholesterol, below levels that matter clinically; authors advise against routine use.
sources.population: 757 adults with BMI 25 or more, mostly with cardiometabolic conditions

sources.citation: Alebrahim H, Alsaei A, Sefen P, Hasan M, Ramadhan A, Deen GR. The health benefits of alkaline water: is it a fact or marketing myth? Front Med. 2026.
sources.finding: Alkaline water shows modest, mineral-driven effects on reflux and hydration markers; claims of body alkalinisation, immunity or anti-ageing lack robust clinical evidence.

sources.citation: Shahmohammadi F, Khosroshahi RA, Derakhshanian H, Mohammadi H. Vinegar consumption and health: an umbrella review of meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials. Food Sci Nutr. 2026.
sources.finding: Re-pooling 38 RCTs, vinegar modestly lowered fasting and post-meal glucose, HbA1c, weight (about 1 kg) and systolic pressure; many trials were small and poorly blinded.
sources.population: Adults, mostly with type 2 diabetes or overweight; some healthy

sources.citation: Castagna A, Ferro Y, Noto FR, et al. Effect of apple cider vinegar intake on body composition in humans with type 2 diabetes and/or overweight: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Nutrients. 2025;17(18):3000.
sources.finding: Ten short RCTs found small drops in weight, BMI and waist; the pool includes a Lebanese trial later retracted.
sources.population: 789 adults with overweight, obesity or type 2 diabetes

sources.citation: Arjmandfard D, et al. Effects of apple cider vinegar on glycemic control and insulin sensitivity in patients with type 2 diabetes: a GRADE-assessed systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of controlled clinical trials. Front Nutr. 2025;12:1528383.
sources.finding: Across seven trials in type 2 diabetes, apple cider vinegar lowered fasting blood sugar by about 22 mg/dL and HbA1c.

sources.citation: Willershausen I, Weyer V, Schulte D, et al. In vitro study on dental erosion caused by different vinegar varieties using an electron microprobe. Clin Lab. 2014.
sources.finding: Soaking enamel in vinegars released minerals; the most erosive caused about 20% mineral loss near the surface within four hours.
sources.population: Human enamel samples from extracted wisdom teeth

sources.citation: Semnani-Azad Z, Khan TA, Chiavaroli L, et al. Intermittent fasting strategies and their effects on body weight and other cardiometabolic risk factors: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials. BMJ. 2025.
sources.finding: All fasting patterns and steady calorie cutting lowered weight versus eating freely; only alternate-day fasting edged out calorie cutting, by about 1.3 kg.

sources.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Choosing Home Water Filters. cdc.gov, 10 Apr 2024.
sources.finding: Test water first; if it has no harmful germs or chemicals a filter may not be needed. Pitcher filters mainly improve taste.
sources.population: US households on public water or private wells

sources.citation: Purchase JM, Villalona C, Katner A, Pieper K, Edwards M. Household point-of-use faucet filters for lead removal: field performance and user experiences. ACS ES&T Water. 2025.
sources.finding: Lead-certified faucet filters cut lead below 1 ug/L in occupied homes; a disturbed lead pipe overwhelmed them, and iron clogged them early.

sources.citation: Hazzazi LW, Soto-Rojas AE, Martinez-Mier EA, Nassar HM, Eckert GJ, Lippert F. The effect of water filter pitchers on the mineral concentration of tap water. J Public Health Dent. 2025.
sources.finding: Nine popular pitchers changed minerals very differently; none fully removed fluoride, despite three makers claiming so.
sources.population: Nine consumer water filter pitchers tested on tap water

sources.citation: St-Onge MP, Roberts A, Shechter A, Choudhury AR. Fiber and saturated fat are associated with sleep arousals and slow wave sleep. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.
sources.finding: On a free-eating day, a higher share of energy from sugar was linked to more sleep arousals; more fibre linked to deeper sleep.
sources.population: 26 normal-weight adults aged 30 to 45, inpatient study

sources.citation: Linus Pauling Institute, Oregon State University. Chlorophyll and Chlorophyllins. Micronutrient Information Center (updated 2021, reviewed 2022).
sources.finding: Most supplements are copper chlorophyllin. Skin evidence is two ten-person gel pilots; odour results are mixed; untested in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
sources.population: Human studies and case reports reviewed

sources.citation: Juurlink DN. Activated charcoal for acute overdose: a reappraisal. Br J Clin Pharmacol. 2016.
sources.finding: Activated charcoal binds many drugs in the gut and reduces their absorption, the basis for its use in overdoses; it is not risk-free.

sources.citation: Suarez FL, Furne J, Springfield J, Levitt MD. Failure of activated charcoal to reduce the release of gases produced by the colonic flora. Am J Gastroenterol. 1999.
sources.finding: A week of activated charcoal four times daily did not reduce sulfur gases, total gas release or abdominal symptoms.

sources.citation: Di Stefano M, Strocchi A, Malservisi S, et al. Non-absorbable antibiotics for managing intestinal gas production and gas-related symptoms. Aliment Pharmacol Ther. 2000.
sources.finding: In a double-blind trial, activated charcoal 400 mg twice daily did not lower gas production or symptoms; rifaximin did.

sources.citation: Elomaa K, Ranta S, Tuominen J, Lahteenmaki P. Charcoal treatment and risk of escape ovulation in oral contraceptive users. Hum Reprod. 2001.
sources.finding: Charcoal taken 3 hours after, and at least 12 hours before, the pill caused no ovulation in pill users.

sources.citation: Lee SY, Park KH, Choi JW, et al. A prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded, and split-face clinical study on LED phototherapy for skin rejuvenation. J Photochem Photobiol B. 2007;88(1):51-67.
sources.finding: Clinic LED at 830 nm, 633 nm or both, twice weekly for four weeks, reduced measured wrinkles by up to 36% and raised elasticity up to 19% from baseline.

sources.citation: Wunsch A, Matuschka K. A controlled trial to determine the efficacy of red and near-infrared light treatment in patient satisfaction, reduction of fine lines, wrinkles, skin roughness, and intradermal collagen density increase. Photomed Laser Surg. 2014;32(2):93-100.
sources.finding: Thirty full-body red or broad-spectrum light sessions improved blinded wrinkle ratings, roughness and ultrasound collagen versus untreated controls, who were not randomized. Fully sponsor-funded.
sources.population: 136 adults, Germany; controls mostly sponsor employees

sources.citation: Ershadi S, Barbieri JS. At-home LED devices for the treatment of acne vulgaris: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Dermatol. 2025;161(5):552-555.
sources.finding: Six randomized trials of home red and/or blue LED devices found about 45% greater reduction in acne lesions than controls, with moderate to high heterogeneity and mild side effects.
sources.population: 216 people aged 12 to 50 with mild to moderate acne

sources.citation: Grimes DR. Methodological issues in visible LED therapy dermatological research and reporting. PLoS One. 2025;20(9):e0332995.
sources.finding: Of 27 LED skin studies, only a third had both a non-light control and blinded assessment; 37% were manufacturer-sponsored. Efficacy evidence is described as mixed.

sources.citation: Bu P, Duan R, Luo J, Yang T, Liu N, Wen C. Development of home beauty devices for facial rejuvenation: establishment of efficacy evaluation system. Clin Cosmet Investig Dermatol. 2024;17:553-563.
sources.finding: Evidence for home LED and microcurrent devices is far from sufficient: few randomized trials, small samples, follow-up of 12 weeks or less. The only microcurrent trial cited tested neuromuscular stimulation.
sources.population: published studies of home facial devices

sources.citation: American Academy of Dermatology. Is red light therapy right for your skin? aad.org, last updated 2024-09-13.
sources.finding: Red light may subtly improve fine lines; home devices are weaker and hard to judge. Caution with light-sensitive conditions, photosensitizing medicines, or darker skin prone to dark spots.

sources.citation: Layne MR, Weiser JA. The safety and efficacy of at-home devices for skin care. Facial Plast Surg. 2026;42(5):571-578.
sources.finding: Small studies suggest home LED, radiofrequency and microcurrent devices give modest, gradual results, weaker than in-office equipment, with a favorable safety profile.
sources.population: published studies of home skin devices

sources.citation: CurrentBody. LED Red Light Therapy Face Mask: Series 3, US product page (brand).
sources.finding: Lists $569.99, 10 minutes 3 to 5 times weekly; warns against use with photosensitizing medicines, lupus or eye conditions, and in pregnancy or breastfeeding as untested.

sources.citation: Dutra YM, Malta ES, Elias AS, Broatch JR, Zagatto AM. Deconstructing the ergogenic effects of photobiomodulation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of its efficacy in improving mode-specific exercise performance in humans. Sports Med. 2022;52(11):2733-2757.
sources.finding: Light applied before exercise slightly improved single-joint endurance and cycling time to exhaustion, but not strength, sprinting, running or swimming performance.
sources.population: 586 healthy young adults in 37 crossover trials

sources.citation: Zhao J, Tian Y, Nie J, Xu J, Liu D. Red light and the sleep quality and endurance performance of Chinese female basketball players. J Athl Train. 2012;47(6):673-678.
sources.finding: Thirty minutes of nightly whole-body red light for 14 days improved self-rated sleep and serum melatonin versus no light, in a small study the authors call a cohort.

sources.citation: Mito Red Light. Red light therapy devices, US collection page (brand).
sources.finding: Panels listed from $249 to $1,299; suggests about 10 to 20 minutes per area several times a week.

sources.citation: Ahn SH, Hwang UJ, Han HS, et al. Comparative effects of facial roller and gua sha massage on facial contour, muscle tone, and skin elasticity: randomized controlled trial. J Cosmet Dermatol. 2025;24(6):e70236.
sources.finding: Ten minutes five times weekly for eight weeks: both groups showed 2 to 3 mm smaller facial contour measures; roller users gained elasticity. No untreated comparison group.

sources.citation: Miyaji A, Sugimori K, Hayashi N. Short- and long-term effects of using a facial massage roller on facial skin blood flow and vascular reactivity. Complement Ther Med. 2018;41:271-276.
sources.finding: Five minutes of rolling raised cheek blood flow for at least 10 minutes; five weeks of daily use improved the cheek vessels' response to heat.
sources.population: 12 and 14 adults, Japan; one author from a roller maker

sources.citation: NuFACE. Devices collection page (brand).
sources.finding: Lists TRINITY+ Starter Kit $395, MINI+ Starter Kit $250, FIX MicroWand $175.

sources.citation: Space NK. NuFACE Trinity+ Starter Kit product page, warnings section (retailer copy of brand warnings).
sources.finding: Not for use with pacemakers or implanted electronic devices, epilepsy, active cancer, pregnancy, under 18, or over inflamed or infected skin.

sources.citation: Freedman BM. Hydradermabrasion: an innovative modality for nonablative facial rejuvenation. J Cosmet Dermatol. 2008;7(4):275-280.
sources.finding: Six hydradermabrasion sessions 7 to 10 days apart reduced fine lines, pore size and pigmentation and thickened skin; the same serum applied by hand changed nothing.

sources.citation: Heyday. Heyday pioneers membership-based skincare model with high client retention. Franchising blog (brand).
sources.finding: Membership costs $95 to $105 a month by market and includes one 50-minute facial.

sources.citation: Hamie H, Yassine R, Shoukfeh R, Turk D, Huq F, Moossavi M. A review of the efficacy of popular eye cream ingredients. Int J Womens Dermatol. 2024;10(2):e156.
sources.finding: Retinoids, vitamin C, caffeine, peptides and hyaluronic acid show promise around the eyes, but clinical trials of eye cream formulations themselves are notably lacking.
sources.population: published studies of periorbital skin care

sources.citation: Messaraa C, Robertson N, Walsh M, et al. Clinical evidences of benefits from an advanced skin care routine in comparison with a simple routine. J Cosmet Dermatol. 2020;19(8):1993-1999.
sources.finding: A five-step routine with toner and eye cream beat cleanser plus day cream on hydration and some wrinkle measures over four weeks. Run by the brand.

sources.citation: Yuanxi L, Wei H, Lidan X, Li L. Comparison of skin hydration in combination and single use of common moisturizers (cream, toner, and spray water). J Cosmet Sci. 2016;67(3):175-183.
sources.finding: Cream alone hydrated as well as toner plus cream in either order, especially on dry skin; toner alone ranked last. Repeat toner every two hours added hydration.
sources.population: volunteers with normal or dry skin, China

sources.citation: American Academy of Dermatology. Should I apply my skin care products in a certain order? aad.org (undated page; year is the copyright year).
sources.finding: Wash, then any medicine, then moisturizer and sunscreen. Too many products, especially several anti-aging ones, may irritate skin. Use the ring finger around the eyes.

sources.citation: American Academy of Dermatology. A dermatologist's guide to skincare from growing up to glowing up. aad.org news release, 2025-10-28.
sources.finding: A dermatologist says more products is not more; consistency beats a 10-step routine. Acne that has not improved after a few months of store products merits a dermatologist.
sources.population: general public, teens and young adults

sources.citation: Patel DP, Swink SM, Castelo-Soccio L. A review of the use of biotin for hair loss. Skin Appendage Disord. 2017;3(3):166-169.
sources.finding: All 18 reported cases where biotin helped hair or nails had an underlying cause, such as inherited deficiency. No trials show benefit in healthy people; diets usually cover needs.

sources.citation: Li D, Radulescu A, Shrestha RT, et al. Association of biotin ingestion with performance of hormone and nonhormone assays in healthy adults. JAMA. 2017;318(12):1150-1160.
sources.finding: After a week of 10 mg biotin daily, 9 of 23 biotin-based lab tests, including thyroid tests, gave falsely high or low results.

sources.citation: US Food and Drug Administration. Biotin interference with troponin lab tests: assays subject to biotin interference. fda.gov, content current as of 2022-06-21.
sources.finding: FDA keeps receiving reports of biotin causing falsely low troponin, a heart-attack test, and lists troponin tests that still have not addressed it.

sources.citation: Drake L, Reyes-Hadsall S, Martinez J, Heinrich C, Huang K, Mostaghimi A. Evaluation of the safety and effectiveness of nutritional supplements for treating hair loss: a systematic review. JAMA Dermatol. 2023;159(1):79-86.
sources.finding: Across 30 studies in people without known deficiency, some branded blends such as Viviscal and Nutrafol showed potential benefit; biotin alone was not among those listed. Larger trials called for.
sources.population: people with hair loss and no known deficiency

sources.citation: ConsumerLab. Sugar Bear Hair Vitamins: are they worth it? consumerlab.com answer page (undated; year is the access year).
sources.finding: Two gummies hold 5,000 mcg biotin plus several vitamins, about $30 for 60. Testing found over 160% of some listed vitamins; no studies show this formula helps hair.

sources.citation: Vital Proteins. Collagen Gummies product page (brand).
sources.finding: Lists 2.5 g VERISOL collagen peptides per serving, $16.99 for 30 servings.

sources.citation: Dupuy O, Douzi W, Theurot D, Bosquet L, Dugué B. An evidence-based approach for choosing post-exercise recovery techniques to reduce markers of muscle damage, soreness, fatigue, and inflammation: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Front Physiol. 2018;9:403.
sources.finding: Massage was the most effective technique for soreness and perceived fatigue; immersion, contrast water, compression and cryotherapy also cut soreness. Only single recovery sessions were studied.

sources.citation: Moyer CA, Rounds J, Hannum JW. A meta-analysis of massage therapy research. Psychol Bull. 2004;130(1):3-18.
sources.finding: One session lowered state anxiety, blood pressure and heart rate, not cortisol or mood. Courses lowered trait anxiety and depression most, similar in size to psychotherapy.
sources.population: 37 randomized studies, mixed healthy and clinical adults

sources.citation: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health. Massage therapy: what you need to know. nccih.nih.gov, last updated May 2019.
sources.finding: Massage has few risks with a trained therapist; rare serious harms include blood clots, nerve injury and fractures, mostly with vigorous deep tissue work.

sources.citation: Costello JT, Baker PRA, Minett GM, Bieuzen F, Stewart IB, Bleakley C. Whole-body cryotherapy (extreme cold air exposure) for preventing and treating muscle soreness after exercise in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015;(9):CD010789.
sources.finding: Four small lab trials gave very low-quality evidence, insufficient to show whole-body cryotherapy reduces soreness or improves recovery versus rest. No data on women.

sources.citation: Legrand FD, Dugué B, Costello J, et al. Evaluating safety risks of whole-body cryotherapy/cryostimulation (WBC): a scoping review from an international consortium. Eur J Med Res. 2023;28:387.
sources.finding: Seven reports described 16 adverse events, four serious, including brain bleeding and aortic dissection. High blood pressure is listed as an absolute contraindication.
sources.population: Case reports and trials of WBC users

sources.citation: Feinstein JS, Khalsa SS, Yeh HW, et al. Examining the short-term anxiolytic and antidepressant effect of Floatation-REST. PLoS One. 2018;13(2):e0190292.
sources.finding: One hour-long float sharply lowered state anxiety, stress and muscle tension in an open-label study with no control group.
sources.population: 50 adults with anxiety or stress-related disorders

sources.citation: Jonsson K, Kjellgren A. Promising effects of treatment with flotation-REST as an intervention for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD): a randomized controlled pilot trial. BMC Complement Altern Med. 2016;16:108.
sources.finding: Twelve 45-minute floats over seven weeks eased anxiety symptoms, sleep and depression more than a waitlist; worry did not differ. Not blinded.

sources.citation: Konrad A, Alizadeh S, Daneshjoo A, et al. Chronic effects of stretching on range of motion with consideration of potential moderating variables: a systematic review with meta-analysis. J Sport Health Sci. 2024;13(2):186-194.
sources.finding: Stretch training moderately increased range of motion. Fully supervised programs showed larger effects than unsupervised, but not significantly; frequency and volume did not matter.

sources.citation: Behm DG, Alizadeh S, Daneshjoo A, et al. Acute effects of various stretching techniques on range of motion: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Med Open. 2023;9:107.
sources.finding: A single stretching bout gave a small range-of-motion gain, with no difference between static, dynamic and PNF techniques.

sources.citation: Ali A, Njike VY, Northrup V, et al. Intravenous micronutrient therapy (Myers' Cocktail) for fibromyalgia: a placebo-controlled pilot study. J Altern Complement Med. 2009;15(3):247-257.
sources.finding: Eight weekly Myers' infusions did no better than a lactated Ringer's placebo on any outcome; both groups improved.

sources.citation: Shane-McWhorter L. Intravenous vitamin therapy (Myers' cocktail). Merck Manual Consumer Version, reviewed July 2025.
sources.finding: No data support energy, immunity or stress claims in people without a deficiency. Risks include fluid overload, heart rhythm problems and infections from poor sterilisation.

sources.citation: Alangari A. To IV or not to IV: the science behind intravenous vitamin therapy. Cureus. 2025;17(6):e86527.
sources.finding: Benefits of IV vitamins in healthy people lack solid evidence; IV routes make sense mainly for malabsorption or deficiency, and oral intake suits routine needs.
sources.population: Narrative review of IV vitamin studies

sources.citation: FDA underscores unsanitary compounding conditions. US Pharmacist, 22 February 2022 (reporting FDA's alert on compounding by medical offices and clinics).
sources.finding: FDA flagged IV hydration clinics, med spas and mobile IV services compounding under insanitary conditions; one IV vitamin infusion led to septic shock in 2021.

sources.citation: Naidoo D, Schembri A, Cohen M. The health impact of residential retreats: a systematic review. BMC Complement Altern Med. 2018;18(1):8.
sources.finding: All 23 studies reported benefits after retreats, but most were small, poorly described and briefly followed, with no data on harms or cost.

sources.citation: de Bloom J, Kompier M, Geurts S, de Weerth C, Taris T, Sonnentag S. Do we recover from vacation? Meta-analysis of vacation effects on health and well-being. J Occup Health. 2009;51(1):13-25.
sources.finding: Vacations gave a small lift in health and well-being that faded soon after people returned to work.

Research proposal; shown together.
Research proposal. Several calm-down practices; shown together, nothing auto-dropped.
Both answer the same problem, a noisy room at night; people often own both. Show together so one can stand in for the other.
All three are paid self-testing that promises personal insight; people who buy one often stack the others, and the value comes from acting on results, so show them together.
All sold in feeds and podcasts for testosterone, libido or drive; people often stack two or three. Shown together so the stack is seen at once.
Sold together as a longevity stack (NMN plus resveratrol); both rest on NAD and sirtuin mechanisms with thin human outcome data.
Both taken for weight or metabolic reasons; berberine has the stronger evidence, green tea extract adds liver risk at high doses.
Mushroom coffee blends usually contain lion's mane; someone taking both is doubling the same ingredient.
Both deliver high-dose biotin; hair gummies are biotin plus a multivitamin mix, so two of them doubles the biotin.

safety.note: CDC calls not drinking the safest choice while breastfeeding, with at least two hours per drink before nursing.
With insulin or similar medicines, alcohol can bring on low blood sugar hours later, so glucose checks after drinking matter.
Heavy drinking strains the liver, so any liver condition makes alcohol a question for a clinician first.
Alcohol can deepen low mood, anxiety and sleep trouble, and interacts with some psychiatric medicines. If cutting back feels hard, that's a conversation for a clinician.
Alcohol interacts with many common medicines, from sleep aids to pain relievers, so a pharmacist check comes first.
US labels carry the Surgeon General's advice against alcohol in pregnancy because of the risk of birth defects.
Distill leaves alcohol out entirely below the legal drinking age, which is 21 in the US.
Safety while breastfeeding is not established, so a clinician's view comes first.
Rare liver injury has been reported, and it was most serious in people with existing liver disease.
In a small trial it shifted thyroid hormone levels, so thyroid medicine calls for a clinician check first.
Product labels warn against use during pregnancy.
With a known heart condition, check with a clinician before high-intensity classes.
Tell the instructor about the pregnancy, ease the intensity as needed, and stop if overheated.
With insomnia or anxiety, a daily score can add worry; hiding it for a while is worth raising with a clinician.
FDA suggests talking with a provider about caffeine limits while breastfeeding.
Some medicines, including certain antidepressants and birth control pills, slow caffeine clearance, so an afternoon cup can linger longer.
Pregnancy guidance keeps caffeine to about 200 mg a day in total, which one large coffee can reach.
Cold water pushes blood pressure up, so with high blood pressure a clinician check comes first.
Tub makers list diabetes among the conditions to clear with a clinician before cold immersion.
Cold shock spikes heart rate and can upset heart rhythm, so a clinician check comes first.
Some medicines change heart rate, blood pressure or alertness, so a quick clinician or pharmacist check is worthwhile.
Tub makers advise checking with a clinician before cold immersion during pregnancy.
Creatine labels advise a clinician check while breastfeeding.
Creatine looks safe for healthy kidneys, but with kidney disease a clinician decides first.
Creatine labels advise a clinician check during pregnancy, and safety data there are limited.
Many creatine labels advise against use under 18, though sports nutrition groups accept it for supervised teen athletes.
One stick adds about 1,000 mg of sodium, and more sodium tends to mean higher blood pressure, so a check with a clinician comes first.
Kidneys that filter less can let sodium, fluid and potassium build up, so the kidney care team gets the first say.
A single energy drink raised blood pressure by a few points for hours, so with high blood pressure a check comes first.
FDA suggests talking with a provider about caffeine limits while breastfeeding.
Large servings lengthened a heart rhythm measure (QTc) even in healthy young adults, so a heart condition means a clinician check first.
Some medicines make caffeine stronger or slower to clear, so a pharmacist can say whether a can fits.
Some cans hold over 300 mg of caffeine, past the 200 mg a day judged safe in pregnancy.
Pediatric guidance says stimulant energy drinks do not belong in children's or teens' diets.
Greens powder makers advise a doctor check while breastfeeding.
Greens powder makers advise a doctor check when taking medication, given the herbal extracts.
Greens powder makers advise a doctor check in pregnancy, as many blends include herbal extracts.
The AG1 maker advises a doctor check for anyone under 18.
With set insulin doses, meal timing is part of the plan, so moving dinner is worth planning with the care team.
Kidneys clear extra magnesium, so with kidney disease a clinician check comes first.
Magnesium can reduce absorption of some antibiotics and bone medicines, so doses are usually spaced a few hours apart.
Meditation now and then stirs up anxiety or low mood; if that happens, a therapist can help shape a gentler practice.
Case reports describe clotting changes and bleeding when melatonin was combined with warfarin.
Safety research during breastfeeding is lacking, so a clinician's view comes first.
Blood thinners and epilepsy medicines call for medical supervision alongside melatonin.
Safety research in pregnancy is lacking, so a clinician's view comes first.
For anyone under 18, melatonin is a decision for a clinician and a parent.
Some medicines, such as doxycycline or isotretinoin, make skin burn faster; sunscreen is fine, since the light that counts reaches the eyes.
With sun-sensitive skin, shade or sunscreen keeps morning light gentle, and a dermatologist can advise on limits.
No studies include children, and taping carries breathing risks.
Skin that stays dry, itchy or cracked despite moisturizer is worth a dermatologist visit, since conditions like eczema can look this way.
Multis with vitamin K can affect blood thinners like warfarin, so a prescriber checks first.
Multivitamin labels advise a clinician check in pregnancy, when a prenatal formula is usually used.
Nicotine nudges blood pressure up after each use; a clinician can help weigh what fits.
Nicotine passes into breast milk, so any plan for it is best made with a clinician.
Nicotine raises heart rate and blood pressure after each use, so changes are best planned with a clinician.
Nicotine reaches the baby during pregnancy, so any plan for it is best made with a clinician.
US law sets 21 as the minimum age for nicotine products, so Distill offers no timing or strength tips here.
Fish oil labels advise a clinician check for anyone with a bleeding problem.
In heart trials, fish oil above 1 g a day came with a higher chance of atrial fibrillation.
Fish oil labels advise checking with a prescriber when taking blood thinners.
FDA suggests talking with a provider about caffeine limits while breastfeeding, and a scoop is a large dose.
Stimulant blends have been linked to heart rhythm and blood pressure changes, so a check with a clinician comes first.
Some medicines make caffeine stronger or slower to clear, so a pharmacist can say whether a scoop fits.
One scoop often holds more than the 200 mg of caffeine a day judged safe in pregnancy, so a clinician check comes first.
Pediatric guidance keeps stimulant drinks out of teen diets, so Distill never suggests a pre-workout under 18.
With kidney disease, total protein is often limited, so a clinician sets the amount.
In 2025 testing many protein powders, plant-based ones most, exceeded a strict lead benchmark, so third-party-tested products are worth choosing.
Retinoids are usually paused in pregnancy, and an obstetrician or dermatologist can say which acid, if any, fits.
With rosacea, the AAD advises skipping glycolic and lactic acids, so a dermatologist is the better guide for this pairing.
Very little of a retinoid cream reaches the blood, and the usual advice while nursing is to keep it off the chest.
A prescribed retinoid stays as prescribed, and any change goes through the prescriber first.
Most experts advise stopping tretinoin and adapalene in pregnancy and avoiding tazarotene, so an obstetrician or dermatologist is the one to ask.
Retinoids are usually paused in pregnancy, so Distill does not suggest starting one.
Acne that has not settled after six to eight weeks, or skin with eczema or rosacea, is worth a dermatologist visit before adding a retinoid.
Heat lowers blood pressure for a while, so with low blood pressure or blood pressure medicines, check with a clinician.
Unstable chest pain, a recent heart attack or a severely narrowed aortic valve call for a clinician's go-ahead first.
Some medicines change heart rate, blood pressure or heat tolerance, so a quick clinician or pharmacist check is worthwhile.
Saunas are considered safe in a healthy, uncomplicated pregnancy, though a clinician check first is wise.
If a clinician asked for a device to watch heart rhythm, keep that one and check before changing anything.
Melatonin lacks safety research during breastfeeding, so a clinician's view comes first.
The melatonin in most gummies calls for medical supervision with blood thinners or epilepsy medicines.
Melatonin lacks safety research in pregnancy, so a clinician's view comes first.
Gummies look like sweets, and lab tests found real doses up to about 3.5 times the label.
With a known heart condition, a clinician check before starting or stepping up hard lifting is the standard advice.
Strength work is encouraged in pregnancy; tell the coach, and avoid lying flat on the back for long later on.
If a sunscreen stings, as can happen with rosacea, a mineral one with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide is often gentler.
A mole or spot that is new, changing, itching or bleeding is one to show a board-certified dermatologist.
Any change to therapy is best talked through with the therapist first.
Salicylic acid is generally considered fine for a limited time in pregnancy, and the AAD suggests checking with an obstetrician or dermatologist first.
With rosacea, dermatologists advise stopping exfoliation altogether, and acne that keeps flaring is worth a dermatologist visit.
A dark spot that is new or changing is one for a dermatologist rather than a serum.
Very high vitamin D intakes can damage kidneys, so with kidney disease a clinician sets the dose.
Vitamin D labels advise checking with a doctor when taking other medicines.
Vitamin D is often advised in pregnancy, so any change goes through a clinician.
Tell the instructor about the pregnancy, pick unheated classes, and avoid lying flat on the back for long later on.
With a known heart condition, check with a clinician before starting or ramping up long cardio sessions.
Trials of cold showers left out people with serious heart conditions, so a clinician is the one to ask first.
Calorie logging is linked with more food worry in some people. With an eating disorder history, check with a clinician first.
Skip areas with a known clot or bruise. With a clotting disorder or blood thinners, ask a clinician first.
If your jaw clicks, locks or aches, a dentist is the one to ask before any jaw training.
With bipolar disorder, bright light can tip mood upward. Worth starting with a clinician, ideally alongside existing care.
Weighted blankets are not safe for babies. For a child, a pediatrician is the first stop.
Strips don't change sleep apnea. Loud snoring with gasping or heavy daytime sleepiness is worth a clinician visit.
Keep the volume low and the speaker away from your head. Loud all-night sound may affect hearing.
Iron is best started after a blood test shows low iron. Extra iron when levels are normal can build up and cause harm.
Iron can weaken thyroid medicine, some antibiotics and other drugs. Spacing the two about two hours apart usually helps.
Above 40 mg a day of zinc, from all sources, can lower copper over time. A multivitamin may already include zinc.
Zinc can reduce absorption of some antibiotics. Spacing the two at least two hours apart usually helps.
High-dose vitamin C raises urine oxalate. With kidney stones or kidney disease, 1 g a day or more is worth checking first.
Metformin and stomach-acid medicines can lower B12 over time. A B12 test is worth asking about.
Concentrated turmeric and curcumin products have been linked to liver injury. Check with a clinician first.
Curcumin can slow blood clotting. With blood thinners such as warfarin, aspirin or clopidogrel, check with a clinician first.
Turmeric in food is fine, but turmeric supplements may be unsafe in pregnancy.
Stop and see a clinician with tiredness, nausea, dark urine or yellowing skin or eyes.
CoQ10 may interact with warfarin. Check with a prescriber first.
Evening primrose oil may raise bleeding with warfarin. Check with a prescriber first.
With serious illness or a weakened immune system, probiotics carry more risk. Check with a clinician first.
